winterskills5.10.description: I have slept outside for two consecutive nights, twice, in winter (including the requirements for previous stages).<detail>Scouts can spend two consecutive nights at a winter camp. At this stage, it is expected that Scouts stay in a temporary shelter that they have built or a tent.</detail>

verticalskills4.7.description:
I can belay using an auto-locking belay device.<detail>The Scout belayer can provide a continuous belay to a climber from the start to the finish (when the climber unties from the rope).

The knowledge and skill of attaching and detaching the belay device to the rope is not required.</detail>

verticalskills4.6.description:
I know what makes a safe and unsafe climbing site.<detail>Scouts can recognize and describe the hazards posed by loose rock, soil and vegetation.

Scouts can describe the hazards of flora and fauna: poisonous/thorny plants, tree sap, bees and ants, poisonous snakes, dead/rotted trees, hanging dead trees/branches, animals defending territory or that may kick down rocks.

Scouts can recognize and describe man-made hazards: power lines, telephone/communication cables, pipes and iron works, litter (such as glass and tin cans), standing water/fluid spills, other climbers above.

Scouts can recognize and describe environmental hazards: lighting, rain/snow, waterfalls/flash floods and avalanches.</detail>

verticalskills4.8.description:
I can name and identify the use of three types of locking carabiners and three types of non-locking carabiners.<detail>Scouts can describe the use of and the advantages and limitations of the types of carabiners.  (e.g. screw gate steel carabiners are good for setting up top rope anchors, but they are too heavy to take along on multi-pitch climbing.)

Locking could include: auto locking, screw gate pear (Munter hitch), screw gate D steel, etc.

Non-locking could include: aluminum oval, bent gate, wire gate, aluminum  D, etc.</detail>

verticalskills4.3.description:
I know how to perform an equipment safety check of myself, my climbing partner and anchor and belay systems.<detail>Scouts can perform a head-to-toe check of clothing and attire (no loose clothing, sharp objects in pockets, untied shoes, jewelry and helmet/harness is properly secured).

Scouts can perform a squeeze and visual check of all knots and carabiners before use.

Scouts can check that there are redundant, equalized and properly loaded anchor systems.

Scouts can establish there is a proper connection/anchoring and loading of belay devices.</detail>

verticalskills4.2.description:
I know the main safety rules for climbing or rappelling at an outdoor natural climbing site.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate where and when to wear a helmet. 

Scouts can demonstrate when to be tied in with a rope, anchored and belayed.

Scouts can demonstrate when it is safe to begin to climb and rappel.

Scouts can demonstrate where to be situated to safely observe climbers.</detail>

verticalskills4.5.description:
I have coiled a climbing rope (any method).<detail>Scouts can coil at a beginner level.

The coil should be sufficient to be carried in a backpack and can be uncoiled in a short time freely without entanglements or knots.</detail>

verticalskills4.4.description: I know the communication calls and script to follow between a climber and belayer.<detail>Scouts can explain when and why the climbing communication script is required, including what specific words to say for the belayer and climber before starting climbing and when the climb is over; what to say if a rock falls; and how, why and what to ask for to change the rope tension during a climb.</detail>

aquaticskills3.1.description:
I can explain common water safety risks and how to avoid them.<detail>Scouts can explain common risks, such as drowning, hypothermia and sunburn. 

Scouts can explain common solutions for risks such as a buddy system, wearing exposure protection and staying out of the water in cold conditions.</detail>

aquaticskills3.2.description:
I can use a snorkel and adjust my mask to fit comfortably.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate the "stay on face" test to confirm if a mask fits correctly. 

Scouts can clear a snorkel partially flooded with water.</detail>

aquaticskills3.3.description: I know how to remove a cramp in my leg with a buddy’s help.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate cramp removal by pulling the fin tip towards themselves, either on themselves or on a buddy.</detail>

aquaticskills3.4.description: I can put on a PFD while in the water and use the HELP and Huddle positions.<detail>Scout can demonstrate the HELP survival position with the legs tucked in and in a huddle.</detail>

aquaticskills3.5.description: I can swim 25 metres in a pool (using any stroke).<detail>Scouts can demonstrate they are capable of moving in the water.</detail>

aquaticskills3.6.description:
I can recognize the signs of a panicked snorkeler/diver and know how to call for help.<detail>Scouts can identify someone wildly flapping his or her arms and gasping for air as somebody who is in distress. 

Calling for help can be something as simple as yelling to attract attention or calling 9-1-1 on a telephone.</detail>

verticalskills4.1.description:
I have tied a climbing rope into my climbing harness.<detail>Scouts can tie a climbing rope into their harnesses using any appropriate knot.

The harness tie-in must be accomplished at a masterly level with the knot tied correctly into the proper location on the harness and the harness adjusted properly.</detail>

winterskills5.14.description: I have a first aid qualification equivalent to the Scout First Aid badge (St John’s or Red Cross Standard First Aid).<detail>Scouts will have completed standard first aid training.</detail>

winterskills5.13.description:
I know how to avoid, recognize and treat carbon monoxide poisoning (which can occur in winter shelters).<detail>Scouts can describe how to avoid and treat carbon monoxide poisoning.

Scouts can identify possible causes of carbon monoxide poisoning related to winter camping.</detail>

winterskills5.12.description:
I have hiked a minimum of 5 km in winter conditions following compass bearings.<detail>Scouts can hike a minimum of 5 km following compass bearings. 

This can be done as a part of the six-hour hike completed for this stage.</detail>

winterskills5.11.description: I have participated in a winter hike lasting at least six hours and covering at least 6 km.<detail>As a part of a Patrol, Scouts can hike for at least six hours, covering at least 6 km. This can be done using snowshoes or nordic skis.</detail>

winterskills5.15.description: I can execute a ladder rescue, chain assist and reaching assist for someone who has fallen through the ice.<detail>Scouts Canada Field Book pages 188-89 describe the required rescue techniques.</detail>

sailingskills2.1.description: I can explain the safety rules for being near water.<detail>Scouts should be able to explain the safety rules for being near water including wearing a PFD, having a buddy and telling an adult that they are going near the water.</detail>

sailingskills2.2.description:
I am familiar with the signs and symptoms of mild hypothermia.
<detail>Scouts should be able to describe the early signs and symptoms of hypothermia, and know that the body loses heat 25 times faster than in air.
* constant shivering
* tiredness
* low energy
* cold or pale skin
* fast breathing (hyperventilation)
</detail>

scoutcraftskills4.1.description: I have completed a Scoutcraft project with my Scout team using at least a square lashing to join two poles at right angles.<detail>Scouts must have a Scouter (or Scout with Scoutcraft Level 6 or higher) inspect the construction before use.</detail>

sailingskills2.5.description:
I am familiar with the three common whistle signals and when they would be used.<detail>While there may be variations to exactly how whistles are used, Scouts should be aware of some of the basic whistle signals.
* One blast means ease the sheets to depower the sails and listen for further instructions;
* Two blasts means tack/gybe and sail towards the leaders’ safety boat or the designated fleet leader in another sailboat; and
* Three blasts means EMERGENCY—go to who blew the whistle and stand by to assist if possible.
</detail>

scoutcraftskills4.4.description: I can use a knife safely (opening, closing, passing, cleaning, caring for) and have earned my knife permit.<detail>Scouts must demonstrate these skills to a Scouter to obtain a permit.</detail>

sailingskills2.6.description:
I can describe five appropriate actions I should take if I capsize in a sailboat.
<detail>Scouts should know five actions in the event of capsizing.
* Stay with the boat.
* Make noise to get attention.
* Count to five and take a breath.
* Hang onto the sailboat.
* Follow the instructions of the rescuer.
</detail>

scoutcraftskills4.5.description: I know how to disinfect water for drinking.<detail>Scouts must demonstrate this knowledge by preparing a minimum of a 1 litre bottle filled with water from a natural source.</detail>

sailingskills2.3.description: I can explain how I should care for my PFD. <detail>Scouts should know that a poorly cared-for PFD is at risk of mold, tears and/or deterioration. They should also know that a damaged PFD will not work reliably.</detail>

scoutcraftskills4.2.description:
I can tie the following knots.<detail>Scouts can tie the four knots to a mastery level with a firm feel for the knot, symmetry with no twists or crossovers in the knot, and with a 5–10 cm tail at the end of the knot where required.

A rope over 8 mm in diameter is to be used to demonstrate the whipping skill.</detail>

sailingskills2.4.description: I can explain the difference between a PFD and a life jacket.<detail>Scouts should be able to explain that a PFD may not hold a person’s face out of the water if they are unconscious, and that a life jacket will turn a person face up.</detail>

scoutcraftskills4.3.description: I can cook over a fire to roast and bake food items.<detail>Scouts can cook (by both roasting and baking over a fire) enough food to be shared with the Patrol.</detail>

sailingskills2.9.description: I have used a throw bag. <detail>Scouts should demonstrate an ability to use a throw bag, but without a standard for how far or how accurately it goes at this stage.</detail>

scoutcraftskills4.8.description: I can safely identify three edible wild plants. (Note:  Scouters must approve all plants before they are consumed by Scouts.)<detail>Scouts can safely identify three edible wild plants in a natural setting and context. Scouters must approve all plants before they are consumed by Scouts.</detail>

scoutcraftskills4.9.description: I can quickly (under five minutes) build an emergency warming fire for a group of three people without using tools (only matches).<detail>Within five minutes (timed), Scouts can build a fire that should be burning sufficiently so that it does not require fuel or manipulation to remain reliably burning.</detail>

sailingskills2.7.description: I can demonstrate how to tie reef knot, sheet bend and figure-eight.<detail>Scouts should be able to tie the reef knot, sheet bend and figure-eight.</detail>

scoutcraftskills4.6.description: I can establish the four cardinal directions (north, south, east, west) without a magnetic compass or any electronic means.<detail>Scouts can establish the cardinal points and explain how they accomplished this task.</detail>

sailingskills2.8.description:
I can identify twelve key parts of my sailboat. <detail>Scouts need to be able to identify the twelve key parts of a sailboat.
* hull
* mast
* sprit pole
* boom
* rudder
* tiller
* flotation air bags
* dagger board
* centerboard
* painter
* halyard
* mainsheet
</detail>

scoutcraftskills4.7.description: I can build a personal sleeping shelter out of snow or any other natural materials.<detail>Scouts can construct a shelter that protects from wind, rain, sun and snow.</detail>

paddlingskills1.9.description: I can explain the risks of cold water.<detail>A Scout can explain that cold water means your body will not function as well as it should.</detail>

paddlingskills1.8.description: I can explain why I should care for my PFD.<detail>Scouts know that a poorly cared for PFD is at risk of mould, tears and deterioration. They should also know that a damaged PFD will not work reliably.</detail>

paddlingskills1.7.description:
I have demonstrated how to behave safely in my canoe or kayak.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate (while in a watercraft) that they must keep their weight low in the watercraft and balance themselves by holding both gunwales.

Scouts can demonstrate that if they are not paddling they should sit on the floor and that there is no jumping, sudden movements or horseplay while in the watercraft.</detail>

paddlingskills1.6.description:
I can demonstrate the correct way to hold my paddle.<detail>Scouts can show the proper use of a paddle with the top hand properly on the grip and the bottom hand on the shaft.

Scouts’ hands should be as far apart as their shoulders.</detail>

paddlingskills1.5.description: I can show where the bow and stern are in a canoe or kayak.<detail>Scouts can tell the difference between the front and the back of a watercraft and know the proper names for the front and the back.</detail>

paddlingskills1.4.description: I can put on my PFD and know how it should fit.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to properly put on a PFD, ensuring all buckles and zippers are properly fastened and that their PFD is snug enough not to slide over their heads.</detail>

paddlingskills1.3.description: I can explain what a PFD is for.<detail>Scouts can show that they know and understand the purpose of a PFD; a PFD must be worn at all times when paddling and a PFD is to be put on before entering any watercraft.</detail>

paddlingskills1.2.description: I can blow bubbles in the water for 10 seconds.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate that they are comfortable putting their faces in the water for 10 seconds.</detail>

paddlingskills1.1.description: I can jump into chest-deep water with my Personal Flotation Device (PFD) on.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate they are comfortable getting into and out of the water with a PFD on.</detail>

sailingskills3.12a.description: three daysails of four hours each, or

sailingskills3.12b.description: six daysails of two hours each.<detail>Scouts should have an opportunity to practise their sailing skills.</detail>

emergencyskills3.8.description: I know the dangers of touching power lines with a stick or ladder, climbing on electrical power poles, towers and substations, and poking electrical outlets.<detail>Scouts can explain the hazards of such activities.</detail>

emergencyskills3.9.description: I know the dangers of playing around storm sewers, construction sites, garbage dumps or dumpsters, ice-covered water or water areas, dams, vacant buildings, farm machinery, quarries, old wells and/or unfriendly animals.<detail>Scouts can explain the dangers of playing near listed dangerous areas.</detail>

emergencyskills3.6.description: I can show how to lock, unlock and secure all windows, doors and other entryways into my home.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to lock, unlock and secure windows, doors and entryways in their homes.</detail>

emergencyskills3.7.description: I know the dangers of playing on or near train tracks, trestles, crossings and train yards.<detail>Scouts can explain the dangers of playing near train areas.</detail>

emergencyskills3.1.description:
I can perform first aid for large wounds.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate proper care for large wounds:
* applying pressure to the wound with a clean dressing (such as gauze)
* securing the dressing with a bandage such as roller gauze or a triangular bandage
* demonstrate the use of the Scout neckerchief as a triangular bandage
* if the bleeding does not stop, applying more dressing and bandages and seeking additional help</detail>

emergencyskills3.4.description:
I know the signs and symptoms of shock and how to treat shock.<detail>Scouts can explain the signs and symptoms of shock:
* pale, cool, sweaty skin
* fast and shallow breathing
* light-headedness
* increased heart rate
* confusion

Scout can demonstrate the proper care for shock:
* putting the person in a comfortable position
* keeping their body temperature normal (a blanket for someone who is cold, or a shady place for someone who is warm)
* getting help and keeping the person calm</detail>

emergencyskills3.5.description:
I can comfort someone who is ill or injured.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate the proper care, including:
* talking calmly with the person
* keeping the person comfortable
* treating for shock
* reassuring the person that help is on the way
* staying with the person unless they need to go somewhere to call for more help</detail>

emergencyskills3.2.description:
I can perform first aid for nosebleeds.<detail>Scout can demonstrate proper care for a common nosebleed including:
* pinching the nose
* tilting the head forward
* keeping the nose pinched for at least 10 minutes
* seeking help if the bleeding does not stop after 10 minutes of pressure</detail>

emergencyskills3.3.description: I can perform first aid for someone who is choking.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate proper care for a choking victim according to the latest methods taught by a first aid organization.</detail>

trailskills5.9.description: I can input a given waypoint into a GPS and then find it.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to use a GPS by entering waypoints and navigating to the destination.</detail>

trailskills5.6.description: I can keep food and food preparation materials hygienic.<detail>Scouts can describe how to keep food, food containers and food utensils hygienic and how to handle food safely during the hike and while preparing meals.</detail>

trailskills5.5.description: I can demonstrate how to use different types of lightweight stoves to prepare a meal.<detail>Scouts can describe the different types of stoves and fuel that can be used on day and overnight hikes.</detail>

trailskills5.8.description:
I can plot a proposed hike route on a map and obtain the required compass bearings.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to plot a hike route and use a compass to obtain the necessary bearings.

Scouts can orient the map using features on a map and use the features to plot a hiking route.</detail>

trailskills5.7.description:
I can use a map and compass to find my position on the ground.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate their skills with a map and compass while supervised on the trail.

Scouts can show how to find their position on the map with reference to their surroundings and local features. 

Scouts can take bearings of surrounding areas and find their position.</detail>

trailskills5.2.description:
I can show what group equipment to bring on a weekend hike and explain why each item is needed.<detail>Scouts can list the basic equipment needed and why and how it is to be used on a weekend hike.

This includes camping, safety and personal equipment.</detail>

trailskills5.1.description:
I can explain how the weather affects the equipment I bring on a weekend hike.<detail>Scouts can explain how the weather can change very quickly and how they need to plan in advance.

Scouts can explain the layering system, outer shell; how to control body head and ventilation; wicking principle. 

Scouts can demonstrate how to keep their pack and pack contents dry in wet and snow conditions.</detail>

trailskills5.4.description:
I can select appropriate footwear for various hikes.<detail>Scouts can describe appropriate footwear and comfort factors such as ankle support, sole support and construction materials.

Scouts can explain the use of gaiters when hiking</detail>

trailskills5.3.description: I can show how to use group equipment correctly.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate proper use of equipment while supervised on a hike.</detail>

verticalskills5.12.description:
I understand the concepts, principles, physics and consequences of shock loading in climbing.<detail>Scouts can explain shock loading: when an object in motion is suddenly met with an equal (or greater) and opposite force, the object (climber) in motion is halted very suddenly; the force of that sudden stop is shock loaded.

Scouts can describe the effect shock loading has on climbing equipment and systems.

Scouts can describe the effect shock loading has on a belayer and climber. 

Scouts can describe how to avoid or minimize shock loading from happening.</detail>

verticalskills5.11.description:
I have set up a 3:1 (or greater) rope pulley system.<detail>Scouts can set up a pulley system that can raise the weight of an adult. 

The pulley system should be constructed out of equipment specifically engineered for climbing.

The system should not be tensioned on a climbing rope beyond the power of one person pulling.</detail>

verticalskills5.10.description:
I know the climbing-specific principles of Leave No Trace.<detail>Scouts in their climbing practice demonstrate the climbing LNT principles.

**Plan Ahead**
* Pick a climb that suits the skill level of your group to minimize the possibility of injury and need of rescue.
* Use appropriate equipment thoroughly checked before the climb.
* Find out about permits and practices; some locations do not allow drilling or anchors, or require permits.
* Carpool to minimize overcrowding at the trailhead.

**Durable Surfaces**
* Ensure the staging area is large enough to accommodate your group; do not forget other groups or users may be also present.
* Use quick draws to reduce wear on existing permanent anchors.
* When bouldering, ensure the ground is durable so spotters or crash pads will not destroy vegetation.
* Removal of rocks or landscaping to make a bouldering problem safe should be avoided.
* Popular climbing routes have established descent trails—use them.
* Do not wrap rope around trees where the friction can destroy the bark.  Instead, tie a sling around the tree and run your rope through the sling with a rappel ring or carabiner.

**Dispose of Waste Properly**
* Pack out worn out or discarded gear (such as old webbing or discarded tape).
* Minimize chalk dust; keep chalk bags closed to prevent spills. Clean chalk spills.
* Human waste is a problem around popular climbing areas. Go to the bathroom on the way to the climb to avoid the problem altogether.
* Soil is often thin with little vegetative growth in rocky, arid or alpine climbing areas. Pack out all human waste. Create a human waste pack-out kit or use a commercial one; burying waste results in high concentrations of human waste catholes in a small, highly used area.
* Urinate well away from the climbing site location; high concentrations of urine at the site make for an unpleasant environment for all.

**Leave What You Find**
* Use removable climbing protection as much as possible.
* Use fixed protection sparingly; for fixed protection, use earth-coloured webbing and coloured bolt hangers.
* Before placing bolts, check with local land managers; it may not be legal or it may be required to use a hand drill rather than motorized drill.
* If climbing a new route, avoid lichen-covered rock, vegetated cracks and areas that require cleaning.
* Leave the rocks in place rather than force a route that will leave a noticeable path.

**Respect Wildlife**
* Critical nesting sites are found in cliff faces for many birds; other animals use rock outcrops for shelter.
* Be aware of seasonal rock site closures (mandatory and voluntary).
* Keep alert for animals protecting their homes; change or abandon climbing routes to leave animals their space.
* Be careful placing hands and feet; do not accidentally destroy a nest or get bitten by hidden wildlife and insects.
* Considerate of Other Visitors
* Consider climbing on weekdays or less-popular times.
* Wear earth-tone clothes to minimize your visual impact while scurrying up a cliff face.
* Minimize noise while waiting to climb or hanging out with your group.
* Give other climbing parties plenty of room and time to climb at their pace, or politely ask if you can pass when it is convenient and safe.</detail>

campingskills4.11.description:
I can demonstrate safe practices around fires and cooking equipment to minimize the risk of burns, scalds and other injuries at camp.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate a consistent and high level of fire risk
management behaviour.</detail>

campingskills4.10.description:
I can assist pitching tent with my team at camp.<detail>Working with a team, can demonstrate how to properly pitch
a tent.</detail>

campingskills4.12.description:
I have spent **12** nights at camp.<detail>Scouts have spent at least four of the twelve nights camping while
completing this stage.</detail>

sailingskills3.11.description: I can de-rig a sailboat, dry the sails and store all the parts properly.<detail>Scouts, by themselves, are able to put all the parts of a boat in proper storage when they are finished with each sailing experience.</detail>

sailingskills3.12.description: I have taken part in at least

sailingskills3.10.description: I can tack, gybe, sit on gunwale, hike, slow down, speed up, bail the boat and balance the boat.<detail>Scouts should be able to practise sailing a boat when on the water by themselves or with a buddy.</detail>

sailingskills3.13.description: I know how and where to get the latest weather forecast for the area where I will be sailing.<detail>Scouts need to demonstrate the ability to get accurate weather forecasts from the internet, radio, marine radio or television, and be able to discuss what the forecast might mean for their daysail.</detail>

sailingskills3.14.description: While fully clothed and with a properly fitted PFD, I can tread water for five minutes, then swim 100 metres using any stroke.<detail>To prepare Scouts for a simulated common accident around water, Scouts must demonstrate that they have the skills to self-rescue within 100 metres of shore, while fully clothed and wearing a properly fitted PFD, by treading water for 5 minutes, then swim a distance of 100 metres to shore. Any swimming stroke is acceptable.</detail>

trailskills1.2.description:
I can dress myself for a day hike.<detail>Scouts can explain how weather affects what can be worn for a day hike.

Scouts can explain the concept of layering and understand what to wear for wet weather.

Scouts can demonstrate the types of footwear needed for a day hike in each season.</detail>

trailskills1.1.description:
I can help pack a backpack for a day hike.<detail>Scouts can indicate the items to bring for a day hike.
Scouts can explain how to pack soft items, heavy items and food items.

Scouts can explain what is meant by “first in-last out” when packing items.

Scouts can demonstrate the wet weather equipment to bring on a day hike.</detail>

trailskills1.4.description: I can follow directions on a day hike.<detail>Scouts can explain why they must listen to the Scouter so that everyone is kept safe on a day hike.</detail>

trailskills1.3.description:
I can list what food to bring on a day hike.<detail>Scouts can explain the food groups to bring for a day hike to sustain and boost energy.

Scouts can show what to bring for snacks.

Scouts can show how to keep drinks hot or cold.
Scouts can explain what dehydration means and can show how to bring water on a day hike.</detail>

trailskills1.9.description: I can recognize the main distress signals.<detail>Scouts can draw and identify the main distress signals (3 whistle blasts, flares, triangle groupings of 3 signal flags, mirror/aluminum foil reflectors, signal fires, SOS with lights - 3 short flashes, 3 long flashes, 3 short flashes)</detail>

trailskills1.6.description:
I can behave safely while hiking.<detail>Scouts can describe safety rules and procedures that will keep themselves and their group safe while on a day hike.

Scouts can explain how their own behaviour affects others on the day hike.

Scouts can demonstrate how to hike on various types of terrain (smooth, rough), how to keep up with others and the importance of always being able to see a Scouter while on the day hike.</detail>

trailskills1.5.description: I can identify the main parts of a compass.<detail>Scouts can identify the parts of a compass outdoors in a practical experience.</detail>

trailskills1.8.description: I can explain the Buddy system.<detail>Scouts explain how and why the buddy system is used on a day hike.</detail>

trailskills1.7.description:
I can be responsible for myself while we are hiking.<detail>Scouts can explain how they contribute to the success of the day hike by being members of the team.

Scouts can describe how their awareness will help everyone have a safe day hike.</detail>

paddlingskills2.13.description:
I am familiar with the signs and symptoms of mild hypothermia.<detail>Scouts can list the signs and symptoms of mild hypothermia:
* constant shivering
* tiredness
* low energy
* cold or pale skin
* fast breathing (hyperventilation)</detail>

paddlingskills2.12.description:
I can identify the parts of my watercraft and my paddle.<detail>Any type of self-propelled watercraft and paddle are suitable.

Parts should include:
* Paddle: blade, tip, neck, shaft, handle, etc.
* Watercraft: hull, bow, stern, bum rest, etc.</detail>

paddlingskills2.11.description: I have used a throw bag.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate an ability to use a throw bag. Distance and accuracy at this stage are not the prime objectives.</detail>

paddlingskills2.10.description:
I am familiar with common whistle signals and when they would be used.<detail>While there are variations to exactly how whistles are used, Scouts should be aware of some of the basic whistle signals.
* one blast—stop paddling and pay attention for further instructions
* two blasts—raft up. If the group is spread out, the lead paddlers should go back and raft up with the back paddlers
* three blasts—EMERGENCY—go to who blew the whistle and stand by. Follow the instructions of the person directing the rescue.</detail>

paddlingskills2.14.description: I have taken part in an at least **two** paddling activities of at least one-hour duration.<detail>Scouts will have completed two paddling Adventures of at least one hour in duration each, and have practised their paddling skills with the support of a more experienced Scout or Scouter.</detail>

winterskills1.10.description: I have hiked at least 1 km in winter.<detail>Scouts have taken part in a short winter hike, wearing appropriate clothing and packing appropriate gear. They have used the buddy system.</detail>

winterskills1.11.description: I know that I should not touch cold metal with bare skin, especially my lips or tongue.<detail>Scouts can describe why they should not touch cold metal with bare skin, including what will happen (skin freezes to metal) and what injuries can result (at worst, some skin remains frozen to the metal, resulting in a serious abrasion).</detail>

trailskills4.19.description: I can help plan a day hike.<detail>Scouts have been involved in the selection of season and location for a day hike.</detail>

trailskills4.18.description:
I have led a leg of a hike.<detail>Scouts can take the lead position on a section of a hike. 

Scouts will demonstrate how to navigate, support, guide and lead others over the trail.</detail>

trailskills4.11.description: I can apply the Leave No Trace principles while hiking.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate their knowledge of the Leave No Trace principles by disposing of waste properly, respecting wildlife, minimizing the impacts of hiking and fire, showing consideration of others and hiking and camping on durable surfaces whenever possible.</detail>

trailskills4.12.description:
I can minimize trail hazards for myself and others that are encountered (trip hazards on the trail, minimizing branch whip while moving them out of the way, etc.) (trail etiquette)<detail>Scouts can demonstrate hiking etiquette on the trail. 

Scouts know what to do if encountering other hikers on a trail.

Scouts can avoid livestock or wildlife on a trail, and know what to do if animals are encountered.</detail>

trailskills4.10.description:
I can cross various terrains such as bogs/marsh or wet ground.<detail>Scouts can explain how to cross various terrains safely. 

Scouts can cross wet bogs or marshes safely and minimize their impact on the environment.</detail>

trailskills4.15.description:
I can identify the different emergency services that are available and how and when to call them.<detail>Scouts can explain how to call for emergency services in the area in which Scouts are hiking (police, ambulance, search etc.).

Scouts are able to explain what each service would provide in a hiking situation.</detail>

trailskills4.16.description: I can build or find an emergency shelter.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to erect a simple emergency shelter or explain natural formations that could be used for emergency shelters.</detail>

trailskills4.13.description: I can be responsible for younger members of my team while we are hiking.<detail>Scouts have a level of awareness to help younger or lessexperienced Scouts while hiking.</detail>

trailskills4.14.description:
I can treat simple sprains and blisters.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate treatment of simple foot or ankle sprains and blisters.

Scouts can explain the difficulties providing treatment of simple sprains and blisters when on the trail and why to avoid these injuries.

Scouts can make the patient feel safe and know how to get help.

Scouts know the materials in a first aid kit that are used to treat a blister and demonstrate their skill.</detail>

scoutcraftskills3.11.description:
I know what makes a comfortable and safe place for a sleeping shelter/site.<detail>Scouts know to look for a smooth and level surface to sleep on.

Scouts know to keep the site out of the wind and (where possible) precipitation.

Scouts know to look up and ensure there are no hazards from falling objects such as rocks and dead trees or limbs.

Scouts know to keep off of animal trails or human walking paths.

Scouts know to keep the site out of low areas where water may pool or run through.

Scouts know to keep a site out of a possible avalanche or landslide path.</detail>

scoutcraftskills3.10.description: I have put together a personal outdoor survival kit.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate a personal outdoor survival kit suitable for a particular expedition, explaining the rationale for the items included and the items left out.</detail>

campingskills3.6.description: I can assist in cooking a meal at camp.<detail>Scouts can assist in the cooking of a meal in a camp setting</detail>

campingskills3.7.description:
I can be safe while cooking at camp.<detail>Scouts can use pots safely to prevent tipping.

Scouts can use protective equipment or utensils while working with hot items while cooking.</detail>

campingskills3.8.description:
I can demonstrate first aid treatment for a minor cut or scratch at camp and explain how to prevent infection and describe the signs of infections.<detail>Scouts can clean a small wound.

Scouts can apply a bandage to wound</detail>

campingskills3.9.description:
I can get a weather forecast for a camp.<detail>Scouts can access information from the appropriate weather forecasters in their area.

This could be from websites, television weather channels or news broadcasts, radio stations or phone apps.</detail>

campingskills3.1.description: I can help others learn about camping.<detail>Scouts display a willingness to help others learn in a natural way over a period of time, rather than mount a single display of expertise.</detail>

campingskills3.2.description:
I can audit my personal gear for camp.<detail>Scouts show an awareness of the value of camping equipment. 

Scouts can explain that if equipment is not working properly, it is likely to fail in bad weather conditions. 

Scouts can demonstrate how to go about checking and caring for equipment.

Scouts can explain the safety implications of poor or dysfunctional equipment.

Scouts can keep personal equipment in working order.

Scouts can demonstrate how to repair items of equipment.</detail>

emergencyskills3.13.description: I can identify some of the poisonous/hazardous plants in my area, and those I may encounter when travelling in Canada.<detail>Scouts can identify in nature or describe some poisonous/hazardous plants local to their area (e.g. poison ivy, poison sumac) and know their hazards (e.g causes rash when touched, vomiting when ingesting berries) and can demonstrate how to avoid their toxic elements.</detail>

campingskills3.3.description:
I can pack a bag for camp.<detail>Scouts can present a packed bag for inspection. Scouts can demonstrate and discuss, while unpacking and repacking: 
*The value of the method used in the packing process 
*The necessary equipment to pack 
*Where to place soft items 
*Where to place heavy items 
*Where to place food 
*What is meant by “first in, last out” 
*What wet weather equipment to bring</detail>

emergencyskills3.14.description: I know some of the international distress signals and when to use these.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate two or three international distress signals for a variety of situations (such as lost on land or on water).</detail>

campingskills3.4.description: I can help plan a basic balanced meal for camp.<detail>Scouts can plan a meal using the guidelines of [[https://food-guide.canada.ca/en/|Canada’s food guide]].</detail>

emergencyskills3.15.description: I can treat bee stings and reactions to some local plants (such as stinging nettle).<detail>Scouts can describe the treatment for a bee sting and exposure to poisonous plants.</detail>

campingskills3.5.description: I can demonstrate how to store food at camp.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate the proper methods to keep food safe in camp (using food containers and/or coolers as required).</detail>

emergencyskills3.10.description: I have made a list of emergency numbers, such as: police, fire, ambulance, poison control, etc., and posted it by a telephone in my home.<detail>Scouts can verify the emergency numbers are posted in a convenient location in their homes.</detail>

emergencyskills3.11.description: I know how to help create an escape plan for a building or activity location in case of fire.<detail>Scouts (working with friends) can make and practise a fire escape plan for a classroom, meeting hall or similar location.</detail>

emergencyskills3.12.description: I know the “Rules of the Road” for safe bicycling.<detail>Scouts can explain and demonstrate safe bicycle riding.</detail>

sailingskills5.25a.description: five daysails of six hours each, or

sailingskills5.25b.description: ten daysails of three hours each, on safe, familiar waters.<detail>In addition to the daysails completed for the previous four stages, Scouts must demonstrate all of the sailing skills expected of a Skipper to ensure the safety of the boat and crew, while sailing in familiar water and winds up to 12 knots.</detail>

winterskills3.1.description:
I have participated in a winter sport (alpine skiing, cross-country-skiing, snowshoeing, snowboarding, skating, hockey, tobogganing, sledding, curling).<detail>With members of their Section, family or through school, Scouts will have participated in a winter sporting activity (such as one listed above).

It is not expected that Scouts will participate in a league or achieve a specific proficiency in the sport.</detail>

winterskills3.6.description:
With a small group, I have built an emergency shelter in winter.<detail>Scouts can build a simple emergency shelter with tarp, piece of plastic, snow or other easily-obtainable items and materials.

(At this stage it is not expected that Scouts will be able to produce an “expert” shelter; rather, they should have had an opportunity to work as a member of a team trying to build a simple shelter.)</detail>

winterskills3.7.description: I know how to find shelter from the wind on a cold day.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate the ability to find shelter from the wind when outdoors in winter conditions.</detail>

winterskills3.8.description: I can pack a day pack for a winter outing.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate the ability to pack a personal day pack for a winter outing.</detail>

winterskills3.9.description:
I know how to watch my fellow Scouts for signs of exposure to the cold.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to identify signs of hypothermia and/or frostbite.

(Please refer to the Field Book for Canadian Scouting.)</detail>

winterskills3.2.description:
I can light a small fire.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate the ability to light a small fire in winter conditions.

The principles of Leave No Trace should be adhered to.</detail>

winterskills3.3.description: I have helped plan a menu for a winter camp.<detail>Scouts can work with members of their team to produce a balanced menu for a winter camp.</detail>

winterskills3.4.description: I have cooked a lunch over an open fire.<detail>Scouts can cook a simple meal over an open fire.</detail>

winterskills3.5.description:
I understand the layering principle when dressing for winter activities and apply it to all activities.<detail>Scouts can explain the principles behind layering clothes (wicking, warmth and wind/wet) for winter activities and have an opportunity to demonstrate this skill.

Scouts understand what clothing fabrics are appropriate and are aware of less-expensive options.</detail>

verticalskills3.2.description: I know when and where I should have a climbing helmet on.<detail>Scouts know a helmet is to be worn for any climbing activity where a fall or loss of body control could result in impact to the head, or when a person or an object could fall onto a climber, belayer or spectator.</detail>

verticalskills3.1.description: I have correctly tied a figure-8 follow-through knot.<detail>Scouts can tie the knot to a mastery level with a firm feel to the knot, symmetry with no twists or cross-overs in the knot, with a 5–10 cm tail at the end of the knot.</detail>

sailingskills5.2.description: I can identify mild symptoms of hyperthermia.<detail>Scouts should be able to identify and treat mild symptoms of hyperthermia.</detail>

sailingskills5.3.description:
I can identify three reaching assists that could be used to help someone in the water to reach safety and have demonstrated how to use one of them.<detail>Scouts must be demonstrated using reaching assists in open water using:
* throw bags
* reaching assists—towel, paddle, pole
* throwing assist—PFD, life ring
* items that would normally be found in a sailboat
</detail>

sailingskills5.1.description: I know when and how to follow the Sail Coach’s commands.<detail>Scouts must be aware of the Sail Coach’s instructions at all times for their personal safety and for making the Learn to Sail session a positive learning experience.</detail>

sailingskills5.6.description: I know games youth can play to promote flexibility prior to going sailing.<detail>Scouts should know three active games to play to limber up and do warm-up exercises before launching their boats.</detail>

sailingskills5.7.description:
I can explain what clothing should be worn while sailing.<detail>Scouts should be able to explain what clothing should be worn while sailing.
* footwear
* hat
* long vs. short-sleeved shirt
* long pants vs. shorts
* all-weather gear
* wetsuit and/or dry suit
Clothing will vary depending on the season of the sailing excursion.

Clothing may vary between different Scout Councils across Canada.</detail>

sailingskills5.4.description:
I know how to create and use a float plan.<detail>Scouts should create a float plan and leave it with their parents or their Scouter as the safety contact at home. The content of the float plan should include:
* where they are going
* when they will return
* who is coming with them
* where the closest aid is
* how to contact them
</detail>

sailingskills5.5.description: I can explain why my boat needs a painter.<detail>Scouts should know that a painter is the rope attached to the boat to secure bow or stern to dock, mooring buoy or tow boat.</detail>

sailingskills5.8.description:
As the Skipper of my sailcraft, I can identify the equipment Transport Canada requires to be on the sailboat and demonstrate its proper use.<detail>Level 5 Scouts MUST identify the five pieces of safety equipment required by the Transport Canada and demonstrate their proper use.
* One life jacket or PFD for each person on board
* One signalling device (whistle)
* One buoyant heaving line of at least 15 metres in length
* One paddle
* One bailer
See the Transport Canada’s Safe Boating Guide for details on all classes of boats.</detail>

sailingskills5.9.description:
I can describe the basic Transport Canada navigational aids on the water.<detail>A Stage 5 Scout must be able to identify the following:
* lateral port and starboard buoys and day beacons
* four cardinal buoys
* special purpose (diving, keep out, mooring, swimming) buoys
* mandatory lights required on sailing vessels underway
* mandatory lights when anchored
</detail>

paddlingskills2.9.description:
I can get help if I see somebody in difficulty on the water.<detail>If Scouts see someone in difficulty on the water, they know to call for help by whistling and yelling.

Scouts can use a throwing assist if one is available.</detail>

paddlingskills2.8.description: I have explained some of the ways that paddling a canoe or kayak can have a negative impact on the environment where I am paddling.<detail>Scouts should have an awareness of the fact that paddling can have a negative impact on the environment and the need to be respectful of the places where we paddle to minimize our impact.</detail>

paddlingskills2.7.description:
I can list the appropriate action I should take if I capsize in a canoe or kayak.<detail>Scouts need to know that when their watercraft capsizes they should to the following:
* stay with your watercraft
* make noise to get attention
* count to five and take a breath
* hang onto your paddle if you can
* follow the instructions of your rescuer</detail>

paddlingskills2.6.description: I can explain the safety rules for being near water.<detail>Scouts can explain basic safety rules for common hazards including: slippery rocks, sharp objects, unstable banks, moving water, etc.</detail>

paddlingskills2.5.description:
I can identify the equipment Transport Canada requires me to have in my canoe or kayak.<detail>Scouts can identify the five essential pieces of safety equipment and have a rudimentary idea of how to use them.
* PFD
* Signaling Device (whistle)
* Floating Rope
* Paddle
* Bailer

Scouts can explain the use of a flashlight for fog or nighttime paddling.</detail>

paddlingskills2.4.description: I can explain why I should not drink the water from the lake or river I am paddling on until it has been filtered or treated.<detail>Scouts understand that lake and river water may not be safe to drink due to bacteria, chemicals, parasites and germs that may be present in the water.</detail>

paddlingskills2.3.description: Before I launch my watercraft, I can show where I am allowed to go canoeing or kayaking.<detail>Scouts can explain where they are allowed to paddle, as they have been instructed by the person in charge of the paddling activity.</detail>

paddlingskills2.2.description: I can explain the difference between a PFD and a life jacket.<detail>Scouts can explain that a PFD may not hold a person’s face out of the water if the person is unconscious and that a life jacket will turn a person face up.</detail>

paddlingskills2.1.description: I can swim 25 metres with my PFD on.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate that they are comfortable in the water and able to swim a short distance with a PFD on. Any swimming stroke is acceptable.</detail>

aquaticskills4.1.description: I have achieved Aquaquest Stage 6, YMCA Swimmer Level, Red Cross Swim Kids Stage 5, or I can demonstrate equivalent skills.<detail>Scouts can provide proof of external qualification or demonstrate comparable skills to a qualified individual.</detail>

aquaticskills4.2.description: I can free dive with snorkel and mask to 1.5 metres and fetch an item from the bottom, and clear my snorkel upon surfacing—without lifting my head out of the water.<detail>Scouts can fetch the object without a time limit.</detail>

aquaticskills4.3.description: I can explain the hazards of shallow water blackout.<detail>Scouts can explain what shallow water blackout is and the steps that can be taken to prevent it.</detail>

aquaticskills4.4.description: I know what gear is necessary for a water-based snorkel adventure, including protective clothing, masks and sunscreen.<detail>Scouts can describe the equipment and why it is required.</detail>

aquaticskills4.5.description: I know how to select a safe place to snorkel.<detail>Scouts can describe what make a snorkel site safe: it is away from boat traffic, swells, surge, marine hazards, etc.</detail>

aquaticskills4.6.description: I have snorkeled in open water and observed at least one marine/aquatic creature.<detail>Scouts have been out for at least a half-day snorkel Adventure.</detail>

aquaticskills4.7.description: I know why ear equalization is necessary when snorkelling/diving at depth.<detail>Scouts can describe why it is important to know how to equalize.</detail>

emergencyskills4.7.description:
I can manage a home emergency situation.<detail>Scouts can explain what to do if:
* the lights go out
* a fuse blows or circuit breaker trips
* a water pipe bursts
* they smell natural gas
* a drain backs up
* a fire or carbon monoxide alarm goes off</detail>

emergencyskills4.8.description: I know where my local community emergency shelter is located or how to find out where a community emergency shelter is located if one is needed.<detail>Scouts can report the local community emergency shelter information to their Patrols.</detail>

emergencyskills4.5.description:
I can help reduce the risk of fire and burns in the home.<detail>Scouts can check that:
* paint, paper, rags and flammables are away from heat
* hot water tank is set below 54°C (130°F) to help prevent scalding
* stove-top pot handles are turned away from the front of the stove</detail>

emergencyskills4.6.description: I can show how to test and care for a smoke alarm.<detail>Scouts will demonstrate with a smoke alarm.</detail>

emergencyskills4.9.description: I know what is in our Group first aid kit and know how to use the kit.<detail>Scouts can take out the Group first aid kit before an outing and review the contents with the outing group.</detail>

emergencyskills4.3.description:
I know the first aid treatment for dirt in an eye.<detail>Scouts can explain:
* not rubbing the eye
* blinking fast
* if there is still something in the eye, flushing the eye under running water (with the affected eye towards the ground)
* getting medical assistance quickly if material remains in the eye</detail>

emergencyskills4.4.description: I know what goes into our home first aid kit.<detail>Scouts can describe the items in the kit to their Patrols.</detail>

emergencyskills4.1.description: I can place someone into the recovery (safe airway) position.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate placing someone in the recovery position, including care for an unconscious person.</detail>

emergencyskills4.2.description:
I can provide care for someone who is poisoned.<detail>Scouts can explain:
* not giving the person anything to eat or drink
* finding out what the poison was
* calling the local Poison Control number or 9-1-1</detail>

sailingskills1.2.description:
I can explain what a Personal Flotation Device (PFD) is for.<detail>Scouts will show that they know and understand the purpose of a PFD.

A PFD must be worn all times when sailing, and a PFD is to be put on before entering any watercraft.</detail>

sailingskills1.3.description: I can put on my PFD and know how it should fit.<detail>Scouts will demonstrate that they know how to properly put on a PFD, making sure all buckles and zippers are properly fastened and will make sure that their PFD is snug enough not to slide over their heads.</detail>

sailingskills1.1.description: I can explain the risks of cold water.<detail>Scouts should simply understand that cold water means your body will not function as well as it should.</detail>

sailingskills1.6.description: I can show where the bow and stern are in a sailboat.<detail>Scouts will be able to tell the difference between the front and back of their boat and will know the proper names.</detail>

sailingskills1.7.description: I can jump into chest-deep water wearing my PFD.<detail>Scouts will be able to demonstrate that they are comfortable getting into and out of the water wearing their PFD’s.</detail>

sailingskills1.4.description: I can show how to avoid sunburns.<detail>Scouts can show how to avoid sunburns by using sunscreen, and wearing a hat to avoid sunburn and heatstroke.</detail>

sailingskills1.5.description: I can show how to contact the emergency services.<detail>Scouts can show how to contact the emergency services at a local emergency number, and to request assistance from the nearest adult.</detail>

sailingskills1.8.description: I can blow bubbles in the water for ten seconds.<detail>Scouts will demonstrate that they are comfortable putting their faces in the water for ten seconds.</detail>

sailingskills1.9.description: I can explain and have demonstrated how to behave safely in my sailboat.<detail>Scouts will demonstrate, while in a boat, that they must keep their weight low in the boat and are able to balance themselves by holding the gunwales. They should also demonstrate that if they are not sailing that they should sit on the floor and that there should not be any jumping, sudden movements or horseplay while in the boat.</detail>

sailingskills2.10.description: I can lift a boat with help from others, rig a sailboat, and practise getting into and out of my boat safely.<detail>Scouts will demonstrate how to rig a sailboat while ashore, then demonstrate how to get into and out of their sailboat safely, how to dry tack, hold the tiller and hold the mainsheet while in shallow water.</detail>

sailingskills2.11.description: Before I launch my boat, I can show where I am allowed to go sailing.<detail>Scouts need to know, and be able to explain, where they are allowed to sail as they have been instructed by the person in charge of the sailing activity.</detail>

sailingskills2.14.description: I have taken part in at least

sailingskills2.12.description: I can swim 50 metres wearing my PFD.<detail> Scouts should be able to demonstrate that they are comfortable in the water and be able to swim a short distance wearing a PFD. Any swimming stroke is acceptable.</detail>

sailingskills2.13.description: I can sail away from dock, hold the tiller, pull in the mainsheet, ease the sheets, and sail straight for one minute.<detail>Scouts should be able to practise sailing a boat when on the water with a buddy.</detail>

verticalskills3.8.description:
I know the safety rules for participating on an aerial/ropes challenge course.<detail>Scouts climb under supervision and with permission from the challenge course instructor.

Scouts follow the challenge course instructors’ directions and the safety rules for the site.

Scouts always wear climbing helmets.

Scouts are supportive and do not distract others.

Scouts respect and look after the equipment.</detail>

verticalskills3.7.description: I can put on and adjust a climbing harness.<detail>Scouts can put a harness on with the leg loops and waist belt adjusted properly and securely tightened.</detail>

verticalskills3.9.description:
I know the difference between the following climbing methods: 
* single-pitch
* multi-pitch
* top-rope
* lead
* seconding<detail>Scouts can describe what is happening with the rope, belayer and the climber in each of these five climbing methods.</detail>

verticalskills3.4.description: I know how to care for, handle and store a climbing rope, harness, helmet and climbing webbing.<detail>Scouts can describe the care and handling of climbing equipment, including storage in a clean dry place out of direct sunlight; eliminating exposure to ANY petroleum products or ANY chemicals (such as battery acid); preventing the growth of mold on equipment; inspection by sight and feel of all equipment at every use, looking for damage, wear, discolouration and incompleteness; preventing participants from standing on, throwing down or dropping equipment; and ensuring the equipment is only used for its intended purpose.</detail>

verticalskills3.3.description: I know the safety rules for climbing/rappelling at an artificial climbing wall.<detail>Scouts can describe the safety rules for climbing/rappelling on an artificial wall, including supervision by a qualified instructor; the importance of climbers, belayers and spectators wearing helmets; careful inspection of knots, harnesses and belays before beginning to climb; prohibition of horseplay in the climbing vicinity; and the importance of being belayed when climbing.</detail>

verticalskills3.6.description: I have completed a climb to the top of an artificial climbing wall.<detail>Scouts (using a top rope climbing method) can climb to the top of a climbing wall under their own power.</detail>

verticalskills3.5.description:
I know the basic outdoor Leave No Trace rules for an outdoor climbing site.<detail>Scouts can list the seven principles of Leave No Trace.

Scouts do not disturb any flora or fauna to set up a climb or use a climbing site.</detail>

trailskills2.1.description:
I know what gear to bring depending on the weather.<detail>Scouts can explain how weather varies from one location to another (from flat urban areas to wooded areas, valleys to hilltops) and how that will affect what gear to bring on a day hike.

Scouts can explain the gear needed for downpour, high winds, sun and humidity.

Scouts can explain the importance of bringing personal protection materials needed for insects and sun.</detail>

trailskills2.3.description:
I can read a simple map.<detail>Scouts can read a simply drawn map of the neighbourhood (e.g. meeting area, local park etc.). Scouts can demonstrate how to orient a map and how to follow a simple route around the map.

Scouts can explain how different colours on a map define the areas (water, urban, park, forest) and can identify symbols used for roads, trails, buildings, rivers, etc.</detail>

trailskills2.2.description:
I can show how to take care of all personal gear needed for a day hike.<detail>Scouts can explain the value of gear needed for hikes and the importance of caring for it. Scouts can check their equipment prior to the hike.

Scouts show how to put away and store equipment after the hike.</detail>

emergencyskills2.15.description: I can find a safe place in bad weather.<detail>Scouts can describe the best place to go in case of a thunder and lightning storm, rain, snow, cold, heat, and/or severe wind.</detail>

emergencyskills2.14.description: I know some of the wild animals in my area and how to be safe around them.<detail>Scouts know what wildlife could be dangerous in the area and how best to react when they come into contact with these animals.</detail>

emergencyskills2.13.description: I can dress myself appropriately for the weather.<detail>Scouts consistently demonstrate wearing the appropriate clothing for all weather conditions.</detail>

emergencyskills2.12.description: I wear my helmet when using my bicycle, skateboard or scooter.<detail>Scouts consistently wear a properly fitted helmet when riding a bicycle, skateboard or scooter.</detail>

campingskills5.17.description: I have spent **18** nights at camp.<detail>Scouts have spent at least six of the 18 nights at camp while completing this stage, including one night of lightweight camping.</detail>

campingskills5.15.description: I can show best layout for a campsite and explain my reasons.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how and where camp equipment is set up at a campsite (i.e. kitchen, tents, shelter, chopping area).</detail>

campingskills5.16.description: I can light, maintain and use a fire to cook a balanced meal at camp.<detail>Scouts can prepare a complete meal (not just one menu item)</detail>

emergencyskills2.11.description:
I know the hazards of water sources in my local area.<detail>Scouts can explain the dangers of getting too close to creeks, streams, rivers, lakes and other bodies of water in all seasons.

Scouts know to have a responsible adult present when swimming and to never swim or play in water alone.</detail>

emergencyskills2.10.description:
I can direct a responder to a location where help is needed.<detail>Scouts can lead or direct responders to the specific location where help is needed.

A practice drill can be used to show this skill.</detail>

trailskills2.9.description:
I can explain why you bring certain foods and drinks on hikes.<detail>Scouts can explain the need for sustaining and energy foods.

Scouts can help plan the food items for a day hike.

Some food considerations include: [[https://food-guide.canada.ca/en/|Canada’s food guide]], high energy; water; carbohydrates, weight considerations, cooking equipment.</detail>

trailskills2.8.description: I have attended at least **five** hikes.<detail>Scouts have attended at least five hikes (including those completed at the previous stages) in natural areas such as parks, forests and Scout camps.</detail>

trailskills2.5.description:
I can obtain a weather forecast.<detail>Scouts can list methods to obtain a weather forecast.
Scouts can explain why Scouts need to watch forecasts ahead of a hike.</detail>

scoutcraftskills4.2e.description: Whip the end of a rope

trailskills2.4.description:
I can use a compass to find basic directions.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate basic use of the compass: how to take a bearing and how to follow a bearing.

Scouts can demonstrate how to use a map and compass together to navigate an area.</detail>

trailskills2.7.description:
I can get help if someone is hurt.<detail>Scouts can recognize when someone is injured and needs help.

Scouts can explain how to get help in various conditions.</detail>

trailskills2.6.description:
I can be a responsible member of my team while we are hiking.<detail>Scouts can identify some risk concerns that might be present on a day hike and offer safety procedures to counteract them.
Scouts can explain how to be a member of the team while on a hike and how their behaviour will impact the hike and experience of others.</detail>

campingskills5.13.description: I can demonstrate measures to secure tents for inclement weather at camp.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to set up a tent properly for rainy, snowy or windy conditions—considering tie-down and staking techniques.</detail>

campingskills5.14.description: I can select a suitable location for standing/lightweight camp.<detail>Scouts can select a location for the camp based on type (standing/lightweight/hike-in/etc.).</detail>

campingskills5.11.description:
I can demonstrate the appropriate measures for minimizing and dealing with food waste, solid waste and human waste, in keeping with Leave No Trace principles at camp.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate the proper way to deal with garbage and camping refuse and how to dispose of it correctly.
Scouts can demonstrate the proper method of dealing with kitchen and human waste in a wilderness environment.</detail>

campingskills5.12.description: I can pitch a variety of tents and shelters at camp.<detail>Scouts can pitch lightweight tents, standing tents, lean-tos, tarps, etc.</detail>

campingskills5.10.description: I can describe the weather forecast and record the weather for the duration of camp.Scouts can use the weather information they have researched and present it to their Troop Leader and to the Troop in general in a clear, concise fashion that it easy to understand.

paddlingskills3.11.description:
I have taken part in **two** paddling activities of at least two-hours duration.<detail>Scouts have completed two paddling Adventures of two hours or more each.

Scouts must carry out most of the paddling with a Scouter or a more experienced Scout (either in the same watercraft or close by to help if assistance is required).</detail>

paddlingskills3.10.description: I have helped a [[badge:paddlingskills1|Stage 1]] paddler learn to put his or her PFD on.<detail>Stage three Scouts can help a less experienced Scout to properly select and put on a PFD.</detail>

trailskills3.12a.description:
at least **eight** hiking activities<detail>Scouts have attended at least eight activities (including those completed at the previous stages) in various terrains, and trail types.

Three hikes should be different from those experienced at Stage 1 or 2</detail>

trailskills3.12b.description: one of which involves hiking on hilly trails

scoutcraftskills3.1.description: I can tie the following knots.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate the three knots tied to a mastery level with a firm feel to the knot, symmetry with no twists or cross overs in the knot, with a 5–10 cm tail at the end of the knot, and can explain a good use for each.</detail>

scoutcraftskills3.2.description: I can cook a meal on a camp stove.<detail>Scouts can use a camp stove to cook a meal for their Patrol.</detail>

scoutcraftskills3.5.description:
I know the first aid treatment for burns from hot water, grease and food.<detail>Scouts know to remove the source of the heat.

Scouts know that immediate cooling of the burn is required.

Scouts know that infections are a risk from burns and can apply the appropriate medication and dressing to the burn.</detail>

scoutcraftskills3.6.description: I have used a compass to walk on a bearing.<detail>Scouts have walked for a minimum of 2 km using a compass bearing and arrived successfully at their intended destination.</detail>

scoutcraftskills3.3.description: I can use a shovel to build a camp greywater sump pit and close the pit when finished.<detail>Scouts can build and maintain a pit at a campout.</detail>

scoutcraftskills3.4.description:
I have boiled water over a campfire and know the safety precautions around fires and hot pots.<detail>Scouts can boil a pot of water on or next to a fire.

Scouts know not to poke sticks or throw trash into a fire.

Scouts know not to leave a fire or hot coals unattended.

Scouts know to use insulated hand protection when working with hot pots.

Scouts know there is no horseplay around fires.</detail>

scoutcraftskills3.9.description: I can lay and start a fire with only matches and materials found in the forest.<detail>Scouts can lay and start a fire large enough to keep three people warm using only matches and natural materials found in the forest.</detail>

scoutcraftskills3.7.description: I can make a personal shelter out of plastic sheeting and rope.<detail>Scouts can make a waterproof shelter large enough to sleep under.</detail>

scoutcraftskills3.8.description: I can identify three wild animal tracks.<detail>Scouts can identify three sets of animal tracks from different species in the wild.</detail>

paddlingskills3.9.description: I can throw a throw bag.<detail>Scouts can throw a throw bag at least 5 metres and be within the length of their watercraft of the target.</detail>

paddlingskills3.8.description: I can make a recognized distress signal.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to make a distress signal such as three whistle blasts or by lighting three fires or putting three watercrafts in a triangle.</detail>

paddlingskills3.7.description: I know what the risks are for paddling in different weather conditions.<detail>Scouts can explain how different weather conditions (wind, rain, sun and cold) can impact a paddling trip and have an understanding of the risks associated with different weather.</detail>

paddlingskills3.6.description: I know how and where to get the latest weather forecast for the area where I will be paddling.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate the ability to get accurate weather forecasts from the internet, radio or television and can discuss what the forecast might mean for their paddling trip.</detail>

paddlingskills3.5.description: I can get back into my canoe or kayak with help from someone in another watercraft if my watercraft capsizes.<detail>Someone else rights the swamped watercraft and assists the paddlers to get back into their watercraft.</detail>

paddlingskills3.4.description:
I have swamped a canoe while sitting in it.<detail>Scouts can rock a watercraft and have it dump.

Scouts do not jump out of the watercraft; they attempt to stay with the watercraft.</detail>

paddlingskills3.3.description:
With help from my team or my Scouter, I can paddle my canoe or kayak forward a short way.<detail>Scouts can paddle their watercraft forward in a reasonably straight line for a short distance.

As much as possible, Scouts achieve this skill with another youth with similar skills.

Adults or more senior youth may be the passenger.</detail>

paddlingskills3.2.description: I know how to choose a paddle that is the correct size.<detail>Scouts can discuss options for sizing and understand that the paddle that "feels right" is usually best.</detail>

paddlingskills3.1.description:
I can swim 100 metres with my PFD on using any stroke.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate that they are comfortable in the water and able to swim a short distance with a PFD on.

Any swimming stroke is acceptable.</detail>

trailskills3.10.description: I can treat simple cuts and scratches.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to clean the wound, apply a bandage and reassure the patient.</detail>

trailskills3.11.description: I know how to prevent becoming lost and what to do if I get lost.<detail>Scouts can explain how to prevent becoming lost and what to do if they are lost alone or as a group.</detail>

trailskills5.18a.description:
**fourteen** hikes<detail>Scouts have attended at least fourteen hikes  (including those completed at the previous stages) in wilderness-type areas.

Three of the hikes should be different from those experienced in other stages.</detail>

trailskills5.18b.description: including an overnight<detail>One of the hikes is to be an overnight hike experience.</detail>

winterskills2.1.description: I have gone sledding or tobogganing.<detail>When sledding or tobogganing, Scouts follow appropriate safety precautions: staying away from roads and other dangerous obstacles, watching out for others on the hill and wearing appropriate clothing and helmets.</detail>

winterskills2.2.description:
I have packed a proper lunch for a winter outing.<detail>Scouts can describe how to make a nutritious and tasty meal to eat outdoors in the winter.

Packed lunches should include as little garbage as possible.</detail>

scoutcraftskills4.10.description:
I know what to do if lost and alone outdoors with no constructed shelter available.<detail>Scouts know:
*To not panic and try to stay calm.
* To call out for help or use a signaling device such as whistle or phone.
* To retrace their steps, if possible—otherwise, stay put in place.
* To try to find or make a shelter out of the wind and precipitation.
* To dress warmly; light a warming and signal fire if possible.
* To spread out visible material on the ground for air searchers to see.</detail>

scoutcraftskills4.11.description: I can set up a tree food hang to protect my food from animals.<detail>Scouts can set up a hang that can support at least 5 kg of weight.</detail>

winterskills2.7.description: I can help less-experienced Scouts to get dressed to go outside.<detail>Scouts can help less experienced Scouts with tying boots, doing up zippers or making sure they have their toques and mittens on properly.</detail>

winterskills2.8.description:
I have attended one overnight winter camp/sleepover.<detail>Scouts can spend one night at a winter camp.

At this stage, it is acceptable for the Scout to have spent the night in a heated cabin or other permanent shelter.</detail>

winterskills2.9.description: I have completed two winter hikes of at least 1 km.<detail>With their Section and/or Patrol, Scouts can complete two short hikes in winter conditions, specifically for this stage.</detail>

winterskills2.3.description: I have participated in two winter sports days (Beaveree, Cuboree, winter challenge).<detail>Scouts have participated in two winter sports days, at least one of which was in support of this stage.</detail>

winterskills2.4.description: I know how to pack extra clothes for winter outings.<detail>Scouts can describe the appropriate clothing for winter outings, including what extra clothing should be packed for a scenario. They can also describe why these clothing articles are appropriate—for example, synthetic fibres will not hold moisture like cotton; wet cotton will make one cold.</detail>

winterskills2.5.description:
I know how to keep my feet dry while I am outside in the winter.<detail>Scouts know how to keep their feet dry by using waterproof boots and staying out of water. 

Scouts can describe why a change of dry wool or synthetic socks is important.</detail>

winterskills2.6.description: When I come inside, I know how to put away my outdoor clothing so that it will dry quickly.<detail>Scouts can describe how to hang up clothing to dry safely (not burning, melting or catching fire) and effectively.</detail>

winterskills4.13.description:
I know how to prevent and treat hypothermia and frostbite.<detail>Scouts can explain and demonstrate how to prevent and treat hypothermia and frostbite. 

Please refer to the Field Book for Canadian Scouting.</detail>

winterskills4.12.description:
I know how to help someone who has fallen through the ice.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how assist in rescuing someone who has fallen through the ice. 

Please refer to the Field Book for Canadian Scouting.</detail>

winterskills4.11.description: I have participated in two 3 km hikes.<detail>As part of their Section and/or Patrol, Scouts can complete two 3 km hike in winter conditions.</detail>

winterskills4.10.description: I have traveled in snow using snowshoes or nordic skis.<detail>Scouts can travel in snow wearing snowshoes or nordic skis.</detail>

winterskills4.14.description:
I know how to avoid and treat snow blindness.<detail>Scouts can explain and demonstrate how to prevent and treat snow blindness.

Please refer to the Field Book for Canadian Scouting.</detail>

campingskills2.7.description:
I can help prepare food for cooking at camp and be safe while cooking at camp.<detail>Working in a team (or with an experienced cook) Scouts can demonstrate how to clean and prepare various food items and how to check that food is cooked thoroughly.

Scouts can demonstrate how to use knives safely when cutting food items.

Scouts can use proper techniques when lifting hot liquids.

Scouts can use proper techniques when lifting hot pots and pans.</detail>

campingskills2.8.description:
I can get help if someone is hurt while at camp.<detail>Scouts can recognize serious injuries and demonstrate how to ask for help.

Scouts can demonstrate how to call 911 or their local emergency number and can request assistance from the nearest adult.</detail>

campingskills2.9.description: I can identify the major parts of a tent.<detail>Scouts can identify the tent, fly, poles and pegs.</detail>

campingskills2.1.description: I can explain the importance of following directions at camp.<detail>Scouts can explain why and how they must listen to instructions, and how to ask for clarification if they don’t understand.</detail>

campingskills2.2.description:
I can list what personal gear to bring on an overnight camp.<detail>Scouts can list the items they need to bring with them for an overnight camping event, including clothing and personal care items.
* Spare clothing
* Eating gear
* Wash gear
* Wet weather gear
* Repair equipment
* Sleeping equipment</detail>

campingskills2.3.description:
I can look after all my personal gear while at camp.<detail>Scouts can describe the value of camping equipment and demonstrate how to go about checking and caring for equipment.

Scouts can explain safety implications of poor or dysfunctional camp equipment.

Scouts can demonstrate how to keep personal camp equipment in working order.

Scouts can show when items of camp equipment are in need of repair.

Scouts can describe the quality of different items of camp equipment.</detail>

campingskills2.4.description:
I can explain what clothing to bring on an overnight camp.<detail>Scouts can describe what clothes they need to bring for different weather conditions.
*Basic clothing for overnight camp
*Layer system
*Outer shell
*Wet weather gear</detail>

campingskills2.5.description:
I can explain how to use [[https://food-guide.canada.ca/en/|Canada's food guide]] at camp and help to plan a nutritious meal.<detail>Scouts can give examples of foods in each food group.

Scouts can give examples of what makes a serving from the basic food groups and can show where to locate the required servings for their age group as outlined in the guide.

In a group setting, Scouts can use the guide to help plan a nutritious meal.</detail>

campingskills2.6.description:
I can describe safe food handling and hygiene at camp.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate at camp how to store food safely.

Scouts can demonstrate how to properly wash their hands.

Scouts can maintain a clean working area while working with different types of food.

Scouts can demonstrate how to prevent spoilage when there is no electricity and how to cover and protect foods and surfaces.</detail>

sailingskills4.3.description: I am familiar with the signs and symptoms of severe hypothermia.<detail>Scouts need to be fully able to identify and treat severe hypothermia, and understand the importance of avoiding hypothermia.</detail>

sailingskills4.4.description: I can describe and demonstrate safety in and on the water.<detail>Scouts need to be aware of local hazards in and around boats, on the water, in known local conditions and in unknown conditions when near water.</detail>

sailingskills4.1.description: I know how to find an appropriate PFD that is the right size and fit for me.<detail>Scouts should be able to describe what is required to find and put on a properly-sized PFD.</detail>

sailingskills4.2.description: I am aware that everyone must wear properly fitted PFD while in a boat.<detail>To ensure the safety of Scouts on the water, Scouts Canada watercraft regulations require that all persons in a boat must wear a properly fitted PFD.</detail>

sailingskills4.7.description: I understand balance in the sailboat and know how to sail the boat flat.<detail>Scouts should be able to describe how to move body position to balance the sailboat and to keep the sailboat flat.</detail>

sailingskills4.8.description: I understand how to trim my sail to get the best performance from the sailboat.<detail>Scouts should be able to describe how to properly trim the sails: where the sails should be when close hauled, and the mechanics of luffing the sail to depower.</detail>

sailingskills4.5.description: I know how to properly secure a towline to my sailboat.<detail>Scouts should be able to describe where to secure a towline and how to prepare a sailboat for towing.</detail>
