sailingskills4.6.description: I know the hazards for sailing in different weather conditions.<detail>Scouts need to know and explain how different weather conditions (wind, rain, sun and cold) can impact a daysail and have an understanding of the hazards associated with different weather.</detail>

sailingskills4.9.description:
I can tie eight knots that are useful when sailing, canoeing or camping.<detail>Scouts must be able to tie the eight knots listed below (time limit: 30 seconds each knot).
* reef knot
* sheet bend
* figure-eight
* bowline
* round turn and two half hitches
* clove hitch
* rolling hitch
* fisherman’s bend
</detail>

sailingskills2.14b.description: four daysails of two hours each.<detail>Scouts should have an opportunity to practise their sailing skills.</detail>

sailingskills2.14a.description: two daysails of four hours each, or

emergencyskills5.6.description:
I know how to deal with an incident, injury or illness in a remote outdoor location and how to summon help.<detail>Scouts can explain how to:
* secure the site and individual(s) from further hazard and harm
* care for the victim(s) and rest of the group
* make and activate a plan to raise an alarm for assistance
* begin an evacuation or establish a treatment site</detail>

emergencyskills5.7.description: I know how and when to use flares, mirrors, horns and other long-distance signalling devices.<detail>Scouts can explain these devices, and the advantages and disadvantages of each.</detail>

emergencyskills5.4.description: I can demonstrate how to safely use and care for a barbecue.<detail>Scouts will demonstrate, by cooking a barbecue meal for their Patrol mates, how to safely use and care for the appliance.</detail>

emergencyskills5.5.description: I have assisted in providing training to others in aspects of emergency aid.<detail>Scouts are able to assist with emergency aid training at a Scout meeting or camp.</detail>

emergencyskills5.8.description: I know how to build a stretcher from improvised materials.<detail>Scouts can build a stretcher from items brought along on a typical outdoor activity day.</detail>

emergencyskills5.9.description:
I can use a compass and/or a GPS device to find direction and travel to a desired location.<detail>Scouts can lead a navigational exercise in the field that includes the following:
* Scouts can read a map and locate themselves on a map
* Scouts can navigate to any fixed point on a map and do so with a safe and effective route plan
* Scouts can establish an evacuation route on a map</detail>

emergencyskills5.2.description:
I can correctly record everything that has happened at the scene of the accident.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate (in a practice drill) a written record of:
* who was ill/injured
* when did this happen
* where did this happen
* what happened
* what treatment was done
* what additional help did you get</detail>

emergencyskills5.3.description: I know the rules and why they are important for a home pool, community pool or a body of water used for swimming.<detail>Scouts can explain the pool rules.</detail>

emergencyskills5.1.description:
I have successfully completed an Emergency First Aid and CPR (Level A) course from a recognized provider.<detail>Recognized providers include:
* the Canadian Red Cross Society
* St. John Ambulance
* the Lifesaving Society
* the Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada
* Canadian Ski Patrol</detail>

sailingskills4.17a.description: four daysails of four hours each, or

sailingskills4.17b.description: eight daysails of at least two hours each, on safe, familiar waters.<detail>In addition to the daysail completed for the previous three stages, Scouts must have completed at least four four-hour daysail adventures or eight two-hour sailing adventures for a total of 16 hours. Scouts must demonstrate all of the sailing skills expected of a crew with a more experienced [[badge:sailingskills7|Sailing Skills Stage 7]] Scout/Venturer/Rover Scout in the sailboat.</detail>

trailskills5.21.description: I can help choose a suitable hiking destination.<detail>Scouts can select a location that meets the desired hiking trip requirements.</detail>

trailskills5.22.description: I can hike on steep trails safely, using appropriate gear as required.<detail>Scouts can describe and demonstrate safe practices for steep trails and list the required safety gear (such as hiking poles).</detail>

trailskills5.20.description: I can help plan an overnight hike.<detail>Scouts can be involved in all aspects of planning an overnight hike</detail>

trailskills5.19.description: I have written a log for at least **two** of these activities.<detail>Scouts can keep the date, route and other details of the adventure in a log which can be added to with each hiking adventure.</detail>

aquaticskills5.1.description:
I have tried an introductory Scuba experience in a pool (Bubblemaker/SEAL Team/Discover Scuba Diving).<detail>Scouts can maintain neutral buoyancy and clear a mask of water while underwater. 

Scouts can open their eyes underwater without goggles.</detail>

aquaticskills5.2.description: I can identify five species in my local aquatic environment (either on the surface or underwater), including hazardous species.<detail>Scouts can name five animals, insects or plants that live on or under the water.</detail>

aquaticskills5.3.description: I can achieve the "Swim to Survive" standard.<detail>Scouts can fall or roll into deep water, tread water for one minute, swim 50 metres—all in one continuous attempt, without touching the bottom or shoreline or side of a pool.</detail>

trailskills5.12.description:
I can describe the dangers of weather on hikes.<detail>Scouts can explain how temperature changes and changes in wind speed and direction can indicate weather changes.

Scouts can describe how cloud cover, mist, fog and snow can affect the hike and how to be proactively safe.</detail>

trailskills5.13.description:
I can plan effectively and recommend appropriate gear to take for my group based on weather forecasts for the hike area.<detail>Scouts can list the gear needed for the hike and the adjustments required depending on weather forecasts.

Scouts can distinguish between regular group gear and safety/ emergency use gear.</detail>

trailskills5.10.description: I can teach a scout the basic use of a GPS unit.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to use a GPS to other Scouts.</detail>

trailskills5.11.description: I can find directions without a compass.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate various methods of finding direction: using the sun, stars, shadows, a watch, the moon.</detail>

trailskills5.16.description:
I can be an active member of my team while hiking.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate awareness of trail conditions and ways to support other members of the team.

Scouts can explain the various roles required for a safe hiking experience.

Scouts can describe proper trail pacing for a group and how to schedule rest and water breaks.

Scouts can explain the role of the front leader and rear follower on a hike</detail>

trailskills5.17.description:
I can recognize and respond to hazards from flora and fauna.<detail>Scouts demonstrate their knowledge of flora and fauna that could be hazardous on the trail.

Scouts can explain how to recognize these hazards, how to avoid the hazards and how to respond to exposure.</detail>

trailskills5.14.description:
I know when and how to cross a river.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to cross a river using various methods, including the preferred safe crossing on a bridge or other designated safe crossing areas.

Scouts can explain safety procedures including how to protect clothes so youth stay dry, and steps to keep warm.</detail>

trailskills5.15.description: I can show how and explain when to use the main distress signals.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate distress signals while supervised outdoors in both daytime and night-time conditions.</detail>

paddlingskills4.12.description: I can describe water and weather conditions that make paddling unsafe and can explain what to do if I encounter them while I am on the water.<detail>Scouts understand water and weather conditions (such as waves, thunderstorms and tides) and can explain the appropriate course of action when they encounter them while on the water.</detail>

paddlingskills4.13.description: I can explain why canoes and kayaks are important to Canadian aboriginal people and the history of Canada.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate (through a group discussion with their patrol, a presentation, skit, story, etc.) an understanding of the importance of canoes and kayaks to Canadians both before and after European contact.</detail>

paddlingskills4.14.description:
I can identify three methods for helping someone in the water to reach safety, and have demonstrated how to use them.<detail>Scouts can identify three methods for helping someone in distress in the water, such as: talking someone to safety, throwing something buoyant to the person in distress, or going to the person.

Any aids identified should be items that would normally be found on a canoe trip and can include, but are not limited to the following:
* throw bags
* reaching assist (paddle, pole)
* throwing assists
* PFD</detail>

paddlingskills4.15.description: I can throw a throw bag so that someone in the water can reach it.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate the ability to throw a throw bag to someone in the water so that the person can easily reach it within a few swimming strokes.</detail>

paddlingskills4.10.description: I can demonstrate basic canoe strokes (forward, reverse, draw, pry, stop, j, sweep).<detail>Scouts can demonstrate these different strokes and have a basic understanding of what happens to the watercraft when different strokes are applied.`</detail>

paddlingskills4.11.description: I can explain why my watercraft needs a painter and can attach one so that it is secure and readily available when I need it.<detail>Scouts know that a painter is the rope attached to the bow and/or stern of the watercraft. They can secure the painter to their watercraft using an appropriate knot.</detail>

paddlingskills4.16.description:
I have taken part in and logged at least **four** paddling activities.<detail>Scouts maintain paddling logs.

The log should include date, location, distance, time, participants and something interesting about each activity.</detail>

paddlingskills4.17.description: I can explain what a float plan is.<detail>Scouts know that a float plan documents: where they are going, when they will return, where the closest aid is and who is in the paddling group.</detail>

paddlingskills4.18.description:
I have participated in at least one paddling activity of at least eight hours duration that includes making and eating a meal.<detail>During this paddling activity, Scouts are tasked with all the paddling.

Older paddlers can be in the watercraft or in a nearby watercraft to help if required.</detail>

sailingskills1.10.description:
I have taken part in a short sailing adventure of at least an hour.<detail>Scouts will have experienced a short non-powered sailing adventure.

Scouts only need be in the watercraft and must wear their PFD properly.</detail>

campingskills2.11.description:
I behave safely around fires at camp.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate care and safety around fires.
Scouts can state basic fire safety rules at camp:
*No horseplay
*No poking at the fire
*Keep a safe distance
*Follow instructions of the person in charge of the fire</detail>

campingskills2.10.description: I can help pitch a tent at camp.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate putting up a tent with other Scouts.</detail>

sailingskills1.11.description: I have participated in a fun physical fitness program designed for sailing.<detail>Scouts should participate in a fun physical fitness program designed for sailing that improves flexibility, builds stamina, improves strength, quickens their speed, and improves their skill level, suitable to the age of the participant.</detail>

campingskills2.13.description: I have spent **two** nights in a tent at camp.<detail>Scouts spend at least two nights camping while completing this stage.</detail>

campingskills2.12.description: I can identify and explain the elements of the fire triangle at camp.<detail>Scouts can explain each part of the fire triangle (fuel, heat, oxygen) and demonstrate the role of each element in a good fire.</detail>

emergencyskills1.8.description: I know how to spot things in my home that are not safe.<detail>Scouts can list a few items in the home that may be dangerous (for example, hot or sharp) to touch, such as stoves, barbecues, fireplaces, knives, tools, etc.</detail>

emergencyskills1.9.description:
I know the different emergency services that are available and how and when to call them and what to say.<detail>Scouts can recite the 9-1-1 telephone number (if applicable in their community) and state the type of emergencies required for calling the number: police, fire, ambulance.

Scouts can make a simulated call to describe the help needed to a 9-1-1 operator.</detail>

emergencyskills1.2.description:
I can demonstrate the basic approach to first aid.<detail>In a practice drill, Scouts can demonstrate:
* checking the scene for dangers (and staying away from them)
* checking the person who is ill or injured only if it is safe to do so
* calling an adult for help or calling 9-1-1 on the telephone
* staying with the sick or injured person until help arrives</detail>

emergencyskills1.3.description:
I can treat minor cuts or scrapes.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate:
* gently cleaning the wound with soap and water
* putting pressure on the wound if it is still bleeding
* applying an adhesive bandage that covers the wound</detail>

emergencyskills1.1.description:
I have made my own personal first aid kit.<detail>Scout’s kit should contain:
* a list of emergency numbers
* an emergency blanket
* 5–10 adhesive bandages (e.g. Band-Aids™)
* pencil and paper</detail>

emergencyskills1.6.description: I know my address and location in an emergency.<detail>Scouts can recite their own address and home phone number.</detail>

emergencyskills1.7.description: I know not to play with matches and lighters.<detail>Scouts can explain why it is not safe to play with matches and lighters.</detail>

emergencyskills1.4.description:
I can be responsible for my own health.<detail>Scouts can explain the importance of:
* drinking water during activities or when it is warm outside
* wearing proper clothing for weather conditions
* using sunscreen when playing out in the sun</detail>

emergencyskills1.5.description: I can be responsible for my own safety.<detail>Scouts know not to talk to or go anywhere with strangers.</detail>

verticalskills2.4.description: I can identify and name the parts of a carabiner.<detail>Scouts can identify the gate, spine, nose, hinge, latch, basket (where the rope sits), crotch (where the attachment connects), barrel and spring on a carabiner.</detail>

verticalskills2.1.description: I have been climbing on an artificial wall or natural rock formation.<detail>Scouts have tried either climbing in the context of a supervised “bouldering” or a top roped climbing lesson.</detail>

verticalskills2.3.description:
I can properly put on a climbing helmet.<detail>Scouts can properly adjust their helmets so that they fit snugly to stay central on the head and not slide forward or back easily.

The chin strap and attachment straps to the helmet are snug, but do not interfere with breathing or talking.</detail>

verticalskills2.2.description:
I know the safety rules for being at the top of or the bottom of a cliff face.<detail>Scouts do not play or get close to a cliff edge unless an adult is present.

Scouts do not look over a climbing cliff edge unless tied in with a climbing rope.

Scouts do not play, rest or stand below a cliff face where rocks, dirt and other things could fall down.

Scouts always have a climbing helmet on when at the bottom of a climbing site.

Scouts never push or throw anything over a cliff edge.</detail>

scoutcraftskills5.10.description: I have dehydrated 1000 calories of food and taken it on a camping trip as my trail snack for two days.<detail>Scouts are to share this dehydrated food with their Patrol during a hiking or camping outing.</detail>

campingskills5.4.description:
I can explain how the type of camp affects the choice of equipment needed.<detail>Scouts can list the Patrol equipment necessary for a variety of camps.

Scouts can discuss how each item is relevant and what safety equipment is required.

With regards to a lightweight camp, 
Scouts can discuss how the load might be distributed among the party.</detail>

campingskills5.5.description:
I can use, maintain and store tools safely at camp.<detail>Scouts can show how to properly maintain and care for the tools being used at camp.

Scouts know how to store the tools for use at another time.</detail>

campingskills5.6.description: I can teach a Scout what to pack for a camp.<detail>Scouts can mentor other Scouts such that they have successfully completed the packing requirements for Stages 1-4.</detail>

campingskills5.7.description: I can plan a balanced menu for camp with a team.<detail>Scouts can create, with a team, a well-balanced menu plan for a weekend camp.</detail>

campingskills5.8.description:
I can demonstrate how to use different cooking methods with different fuel types at camp.<detail>Scouts can use at least two different types of cooking fires.

Scouts can explain the advantages and disadvantages of different stoves.

Scouts can build and use two types of cooking fires to cook a meal.

Scouts can properly use two different types of camp stoves.</detail>

campingskills5.9.description:
I can prepare for and help prevent heat-, cold- and sun-related injuries at camp.<detail>Scouts can describe heat and cold injuries such as sunburn, frostbite, hypothermia, etc.

Scouts can describe proper activity levels and clothing to prevent heat-, cold- and sun-related injuries.

Scouts can seek help for any of the above conditions.</detail>

campingskills5.1.description: I have assisted in the organization of **two** camps for my team or others.<detail>Scouts have actively assisted in the planning of two separate camps for their team or others.</detail>

campingskills5.2.description: I can assist in planning a camp program of activities.<detail>Scouts can actively assist the person in charge of planning the activities at a camp</detail>

campingskills5.3.description:
I can show the personal gear needed for an overnight lightweight camp.<detail>Scouts can indicate (in list form) the items of clothing they need to bring with them for various camping activities over a number of days for a lightweight camp. 

Scouts can explain factors to consider for proper clothes and provision for wet weather.

The weight of the pack is also a concern; Scouts can describe weight-saving measures. 

Scouts can explain the benefits of the chosen equipment design as it relates to lightweight camping. 
*Spare clothing 
*Eating gear 
*Wash gear 
*Wet weather gear 
*Repair equipment 
*Sleeping equipment</detail>

seeoneeaward.C3.description: Complete **15 hours** () of community service as a Cub. //These hours do not have to be completed within Scouting and do not have to be completed as part of just one activity or event. Find your own opportunities to give back to the community in a way that has special meaning to you.//

winterskills1.1.description:
I have built something out of snow.<detail>Scouts will demonstrate an ability to have fun in the outdoors (even in the cold of winter) by building something out of snow such as a snowman, a snow fort, or some kind of snow sculpture.

This can be completed as a group activity or individually.

It is preferable that this be completed as part of a Scouting activity with the Scout’s team.</detail>

winterskills1.2.description: I have prepared a good snack for a winter outing.<detail>The Scout will know how to pack a nutritious and tasty snack appropriate for the outing to eat outdoors, bearing in mind that activities in winter require more energy than in other seasons. Snacks should consider the environment and should minimize garbage.</detail>

winterskills1.3.description: I always carry a water bottle when going on a winter outing.<detail>Scouts should routinely drink water when on outdoor activities and should recognize that being grumpy and tired are early signs of dehydration.</detail>

emergencyskills1.14.description:
I know to "hug a tree" if lost, or to stay in one place if there are no trees.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate in a practice drill the technique of staying close to a tree and staying in one spot when lost.

Scouts can describe how they know that they are lost.

Scouts know to yell and whistle for help.

Scouts know to stay warm and dry if they can.

Scouts know to spread out visible items for searchers to see from the air.

Scouts know to eat food and drink water if they have these items.</detail>

seeoneeaward.D4b.description:
Conduct research as necessary and create a project plan that includes
* a **schedule**,
* a **budget**, and
* an **inventory** of requirement supplies and possible sources for your supplies.

emergencyskills1.13.description: I carry a whistle and visible signal covering when I go out in the bush.<detail>Scouts carry a whistle and visible signal covering (e.g. bright orange garbage bag) with them when in an outdoor setting where they could become lost.</detail>

seeoneeaward.D4.description: **Plan** your project, and assess/manage the risks.

emergencyskills1.12.description: I always tell an adult where I am going.<detail>Scouts can explain why they need to tell an adult in charge where they are going if leaving the adults with small groups or a buddy during an outdoor activity.</detail>

emergencyskills1.11.description: I can signal for help if needed when outdoors.<detail>Scouts know how to make themselves seen and heard for searchers.</detail>

emergencyskills1.16.description: I know how to behave around wildlife.<detail>Scouts show a respect for wildlife and do not do anything to harm animals or their habitat.</detail>

emergencyskills1.15.description:
I know how to be safe around a campfire.<detail>Scouts can state that they are to stay a safe distance away from fire.

Scouts can state that they will not run and play in the area of the fire.

Scouts can state that they will not touch the fire without the help of a Scouter.

Scouts can state that they will not touch tools, such as an axe or saw, without proper training and supervision.

Scouts can state that they will not throw anything into the fire.</detail>

seeoneeaward.D6.description:
**Review** your project, by presenting the results of your project  to your Howler Council, Lair or Pack.

//This is a significant review that's more that just about describing your project and its process.  Your review should also reflect on how the experience of conceiving and executing this project was a personal journey.//

emergencyskills1.10.description: I use the "buddy system" when outdoors.<detail>Scouts know to buddy-up with a friend during outdoor activities.</detail>

seeoneeaward.D0.description:
This is the "capstone" project of Cubs typically completed in your last year before you move up to Scouts.  With the approval of the Howler Council, you will complete a challenging project to address an issue you care about and that will help a community (local, national or international).

//The project may be completed individually, or as part of a team, with the expectation that all Cubs participate fully and share the work.//

seeoneeaward.D4c.description: Present your plan to your Howler Council for its approval.  Your Scouter will need to approve the risk management components of your project.

winterskills1.8.description: I know about the buddy system and why it is used when participating in outdoor activities.<detail>Scouts can describe the buddy system and why it is used, providing some examples of winter emergencies.</detail>

winterskills1.9.description: I know to follow the instructions of the activity leader when at an outdoor event.<detail>Scouts can explain why they must be especially careful to follow the instructions of an activity leader to make sure that they stay safe from winter and normal hazards.</detail>

winterskills1.4.description: I can keep my water bottle from freezing on a winter outing.<detail>Scouts can keep water bottles from freezing by keeping them under their coats or using an insulated water bottle or water bottle insulating sleeve.</detail>

winterskills1.5.description: I have participated in a winter sports day (Beaveree, Cuboree, winter challenge).<detail>Scouts will have participated in an outdoor sports or games day, ideally with their Patrol or Section</detail>

winterskills1.6.description:
I know how to dress to when I go outside in winter.<detail>Scouts should demonstrate a basic understanding of how to dress when going outside in the wintertime. 
They should know to wear a hat, mittens or gloves, and layered clothing appropriate for the climate and conditions.</detail>

winterskills1.7.description: I know how to stay dry or change to dry clothes when I am outside in winter.<detail>Scouts wear clothing made of synthetic fibres to wick moisture and keep dry and warm, or they wear wool clothing, which will stay warm when wet.</detail>

trailskills3.2.description:
I can explain what clothes to bring for a day hike depending on the weather.<detail>Scouts can explain how the weather can change very quickly and how they need to plan in advance.

Scouts can explain the layering system, outer shell; how to control body head and ventilation; wicking principle.</detail>

trailskills3.1.description:
I can pack a backpack for a day hike.<detail>Scouts can list the equipment, including team equipment to bring with them for a day hike.

Scouts can show how to pack equipment in their backpack: heavy items, soft items, last in-first out principle, food items and water.</detail>

sailingskills5.14.description:
I have demonstrated steering a sailboat heading upwind, or bearing off and going downwind, depending on wind conditions and direction.<detail>Scouts should be able to manoeuvre the boat.
* Steer a boat to go upwind and downwind.
* Tack and gybe the sailboat under control.
</detail>

sailingskills5.13.description: I can trade places with my sailing crew while on the water in winds less than 9 knots.<detail>Scouts should be able to demonstrate exchanging places on the water when sailing in light wind conditions so that two youth on board can experience both helm and jib control without having to go back to the shore or the dock.</detail>

sailingskills5.12.description:
I can launch a boat from the dock or from the shore.<detail>Scouts should have the knowledge and demonstrate how to launch from the dock or from the shore.
* To avoid boat damage, the sailboat should be in the water before the sailor gets into it.
* One person holds the boat stable, while the other person slides over the opposite gunwale and into the boat.
* When launching from the shore, stepping into the water is encouraged.
</detail>

sailingskills5.11.description:
I can inspect a rigged sailboat and identify faulty boat parts.<detail>Scouts should be able to identify the parts of a boat that would make it unsafe to go sailing if in need of repair.
* frayed whippings on lines
* torn stitching on the sails
* absent telltales on the shrouds
* weakened swedges on the forestay and shrouds
* loose turnbuckles on the shrouds
* weakened or loose holding fittings in place
* missing or unusable retaining pin on the pintle of the rudder
* missing painter at the bow of the boat
</detail>

sailingskills5.10.description:
I can explain the rules established to avoid collision.<detail>A Stage 5 Scout must be able to understand explain the following consistent with the Collision Regulations Rule 12–17:
* Rule 12 Sailing vessels: opposite tack, same tack, windward tack, leeward tack, downwind tack, tack/gybing
* Rule 13 Sailing vessels Overtaking Boat must keep clear
* Rule 14 Sailing vessels Head–on situation
* Rule 15 Vessels Crossing Situation
* Rule 16 Action by the Give-Way vessel
* Rule 17 Action by the Stand-on vessel
</detail>

sailingskills5.19.description: I can effectively steer the sailboat while sailing flat, identify wind direction while sailing, make the boat turn and head up / bear off within one boat length of the mark.<detail>A Scout, in command of the sailboat, must be able to read the wind in order to turn the boat upwind or downwind, and set the sails properly while underway.</detail>

sailingskills5.18.description: I can work as part of a team to sail in a straight line going forward for at least 200 metres.<detail>A Scout, in command of a sailboat, can sail with a crew as a team to sail the boat properly.</detail>

sailingskills5.17.description:
I have demonstrated making a sail raft and can explain its uses.<detail>Scouts should know how to raft boats together while holding the neighbouring boat stays, keeping hands 30 centimetres above the gunwales to keep fingers clear of being pinched between the hulls:
* with two or more boats in the raft
* for communication between boats or with a sail coach
* for taking breaks on the water
</detail>

sailingskills5.16.description: I have demonstrated proper Man Over Board (MOB) procedures while on the water.<detail>A Scout must be able to sail solo to tack/gybe the boat around, sail back to the location of the man overboard, bring the boat into irons next to the person in the water and help the MOB get back into the boat.</detail>

sailingskills5.15.description: I can demonstrate a self-rescue with my sailboat.<detail>A Scout in command of a sailboat must be able to right a capsized sailing dinghy and re-enter the sailboat by both themselves and with crew.</detail>

trailskills3.8.description:
I can be responsible for myself and aware of my surroundings while hiking.<detail>Scouts can explain how terrain and trails affect their hike.

Scouts can reduce risks when crossing steep or rugged areas as well as in remote areas.</detail>

trailskills3.7.description:
I can explain the effect of weather on hiking activities.<detail>Scouts can describe how weather will affect their hike—duration, pace.

Scouts can explain what to do if encountering severe weather alone or in a group.</detail>

trailskills3.9.description:
I can explain the main principles of Leave No Trace.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate the Leave No Trace principles in action when on a hike, including: waste reduction, respect for animals, minimizing impact on the trail, consideration for others.

Scouts can explain how urination and defecation are handled on the trail.</detail>

trailskills3.4.description:
I can identify the features of a topographical map.<detail>Scouts can point out key features of a map and describe the landscape based on contours, vegetation and water features.

Scouts can explain scale and grid references found on maps.</detail>

trailskills3.3.description: I can follow a route on an orienteering map.<detail>Scouts can follow a simple orienteering trail using an orienteering map</detail>

trailskills3.6.description: I can teach a scout how to find direction by using a compass.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate the use of a compass to another youth including: taking a bearing, following a bearing and orienting a map with a compass.</detail>

trailskills3.5.description: I can demonstrate the basic use of a GPS unit.<detail>Scouts can turn on a GPS and use it to orient their location.</detail>

sailingskills5.25.description: I have taken part in at least

sailingskills5.24.description: I have participated in one daysail of at least six hours duration which includes sailing to and landing at a beach, making and eating a meal, and returning safely.<detail>Scouts and crew should tie their daypacks under the forward deck, then sail the boat to the lunch spot.</detail>

sailingskills5.23.description: I can lift the boat from the water to dry storage, de-rig the boat, and store the sails and foils correctly in the boat storage.<detail>Scouts should be able to safely remove the sailboat from the water for proper storage.</detail>

sailingskills5.22.description:
I can safely dock or beach a sailboat.<detail>Scouts, in command of the boat, should be able to:
* judge the boat’s speed during its approach before turning head to wind towards the dock and stop the boat within one arm’s length of the dock, allowing the crew to reach out and shinny onto the dock
* turn the boat head to wind parallel to the shore in waist deep water, slowing the boat to a stop before both Skipper and crew slide over the opposite gunwales and into the water
* stop the boat before hitting the dock or hitting the sand and rocks preventing hull damage
</detail>

sailingskills5.21.description: I can manoeuvre the sailboat properly while giving the proper commands to my crew.<detail>Scouts, in command of the sailboat, must be able to issue the proper commands in the correct sequence to safely tack/gybe correctly, set a new course and to stop the boat to the leeward of the coach boat.</detail>

sailingskills5.20.description: I have demonstrated how to trim the sail while sailing at all points of sail, including adjusting the sails for wind shifts, and adjusting the sails for puffs/lulls.<detail>Scouts, in command of the sailboat, must be able to read the wind at all points of sail in order to trim the sail to gain the best performance in changing wind conditions.</detail>

sailingskills5.26.description: I have helped a [[badge:sailingskills2|Sailing Skills Stage 2]] or [[badge:sailingskills3|Sailing Skills Stage 3]] sailor explain the basic safety rules for being near water.<detail>Scouts should be familiar with and capable of sharing their sailing knowledge.</detail>

scoutcraftskills2.2.description: I can cook a foil-wrapped meal in a fire.<detail>Scouts can cook a complete foil-wrapped meal, and can describe other meals that could be cooked using this method.</detail>

scoutcraftskills2.3.description:
I know how much water I should carry when on a hike or taking part in an outdoor activity, and I know how to carry the water.<detail>Scouts can fill their water bottles while out hiking and know that their bottles should always be full when they start out on a hike.

Scouts can explain why carrying plenty of water is important.</detail>

scoutcraftskills2.1.description: I can tie the following knots.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate each of these knots correctly and explain good uses for each.</detail>

scoutcraftskills2.6.description: I have helped light a fire using only natural fire starter materials found in the forest, and I know the safety rules for when around a campfire.<detail>Scouts can use a match or lighter to start the fire, but only natural material grown in the outdoors may be used as fire starter materials.</detail>

scoutcraftskills2.7.description: I know why it is important to use a buddy system when traveling in the forest.<detail>Scout can explain that the buddy system is helpful because if something were to happen, a Scout buddy can go for help.</detail>

scoutcraftskills2.4.description:
I know what natural shelter materials or locations are to keep out of the wind, rain, sun and snow and where these may be found.<detail>Scouts can use tree bows, grasses and bushes as wind and weather breaks and covers.

Scouts can also use rock formations and large trees as weather shields.

Scouts can demonstrate how to incorporate natural features and materials into a constructed shelter.</detail>

scoutcraftskills2.5.description: I can identify four trees by direct observation in a wild field, bush or forest.<detail>Scouts can consistently identify and name four trees in the wild.</detail>

scoutcraftskills2.8.description: I know the rules for hygiene at camp (for eating and preparing food).<detail>Scouts know that they must wash and disinfect their hands before handling any food.</detail>

campingskills1.8.description: I can set out my sleeping area for good night’s sleep at camp.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to roll out a sleeping bag, pillow and sleeping mat and show that their sleeping area is organized and tidy.</detail>

campingskills1.9.description: I have spent one night at camp.<detail>Scouts have attended their first camp (this can include the ‘family camp’ described in BP&P).</detail>

campingskills1.1.description:
I can collect small sticks for a campfire.<detail>Scouts can search for and return with some dry sticks for starting a campfire. 

Scouts can separate tinder, lightweight sticks and logs.</detail>

paddlingskills4.9.description: I can make my canoe or kayak turn in the direction I want it to turn.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate a basic understanding of what to do to make the watercraft turn in the direction they intend it to go.</detail>

campingskills1.2.description: I can follow directions while at camp.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate the ability to successfully follow simple instructions.</detail>

paddlingskills4.8.description:
By myself or with a paddling partner, I can paddle a canoe or kayak in a straight line going forward for at least 50 metres.<detail>Scouts can use whatever paddle strokes they wish to keep the line reasonably straight for 50 metres.

Scouts can demonstrate this skill with another Stage 4 paddler, or with a Scouter or more experienced paddler.</detail>

campingskills1.3.description:
I can help pack a bag for camp.<detail>Scouts can assist with the packing of a bag for camp.

Scouts can unpack their bags and then re-pack them, explaining 
what they are doing.</detail>

paddlingskills4.7.description:
I have taken part in a canoe or kayak raft-up and can explain its uses.<detail>Scouts have participated in a raft-up with three or more watercraft in the raft. When rafting-up, watercraft should be touching each other with paddlers holding each other or each other’s watercraft.

Scouts understand that the raft-up is used for communication or breaks.</detail>

campingskills1.4.description:
I can keep my camping gear neat and tidy.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate in a camp setting how to keep things tidy to maintain safety and comfort.

Scouts can describe what would happen in adverse weather conditions if their gear was left untidy.</detail>

paddlingskills4.6.description: I can explain the seven principles of Leave No Trace.<detail>See [[http://www.leavenotrace.ca/principles|LNT program website]].</detail>

campingskills1.5.description:
I can care for my basic personal gear on an overnight camp.<detail>Scouts can explain how to check the condition of basic personal gear and show how to care for it.
Scouts can explain the impact on their safety if their gear is not working (for example, if the batteries in their flashlight are not fresh).</detail>

paddlingskills4.5.description: I have helped a [[badge:paddlingskills2|Stage 2]] paddler to explain the basic safety rules for being near water.<detail>A Stage 4 Scout will have spent time helping a Scout working at [[badge:paddlingskills2|Stage 2]] to learn basic safety rules for being near the water.</detail>

campingskills1.6.description: I can explain the use of the buddy system at camp.<detail>Scouts can describe the buddy system and how and why it is important to use at camp.</detail>

paddlingskills4.4.description:
I can trade places with my paddling partner while on the water.<detail>Scouts will demonstrate the following technique:
* Stern paddler moves ahead of rear thwart and crunches up in a ball
* Bow paddler steps over stern paddler to back seat
* Stern paddler moves to bow seat
* Only one person moving at a time
* Communication between paddlers must happen</detail>

campingskills1.7.description:
I can describe the different emergency services in the camp area and how to call them.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to call emergency services when an accident takes place on a camp.

Scouts can explain the information they will need to provide to the emergency responder.</detail>

paddlingskills4.3.description:
I can assist in launching and landing a canoe or kayak.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate an ability to assist in the launching of a canoe from the shore and from a dock. When doing this, they can demonstrate the following:
* one person holds the watercraft stable while the other is moving
* use paddle to stabilize the watercraft while moving or sitting in position
* avoid damage to watercraft
* watercraft should be in the water before the paddler gets into it
* stepping into the water is encouraged</detail>

paddlingskills4.2.description:
I can explain what clothing should be worn while canoe tripping.<detail>(This competency will vary depending on the region of the country and the season Scouts are paddling in.)

Scouts can demonstrate an understanding of the clothing options available and some of the pros and cons of the different options, including: different footwear, different headwear, long-sleeves vs short-sleeves, trousers vs shorts, rain gear and wet suits.</detail>

paddlingskills4.1.description:
I can demonstrate the HELP and Huddle positions while in the water wearing a PFD.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate the ability to preserve body heat in the event they are stranded in the water for extended periods.

They can demonstrate the ability to maintain both positions for a period of five minutes each.</detail>

winterskills5.9.description: I have helped lead a winter sports day.<detail>As a part of a Patrol, Scouts can lead a winter sports day for a younger Section.</detail>

winterskills5.8.description:
I can use a liquid fuel stove in winter conditions and understand why it is important not to get fuel on clothing and skin.<detail>Scouts can safely use a liquid fuel stove in winter conditions; they can safely transfer fuel, safely and properly set up a stove on a suitable surface, and light and manage the stove.

Scouts can explain safety hazards of using a stove and handling fuel, and how to manage identified hazards.

Scouts can explain appropriate responses to possible emergency scenarios related to operating a liquid fuel stove in winter conditions.</detail>

winterskills5.5.description: I am able to pack the appropriate clothing and equipment for a two-night winter camp.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate the ability to pack appropriate clothing and gear for a two-night winter camp.</detail>

winterskills5.4.description:
I have helped to run a campfire at a winter camp.<detail>Scouts can assist in running a formal campfire while at a winter camp.

This could include laying the fire, running the opening, planning the program, leading some songs or telling a story.</detail>

winterskills5.7.description: I can lay and light a fire in winter conditions for warmth and cooking.<detail>Scouts can lay, light and maintain a fire in winter conditions that can be used for cooking and for comfort.</detail>

winterskills5.6.description: I have built and slept in a temporary winter shelter such as a quinzhee, snow trench or a lean-to.<detail>As a part of their Patrol, Scouts can build and sleep in a temporary shelter that they have built themselves.</detail>

winterskills5.1.description: I have played an outdoor game in winter at least **six** Scout meetings.<detail>Outdoor games at a winter Scout meeting can include anything from tag to snowshoe soccer. An associated requirement is that Scouts come to all meetings prepared to spend time outside (regardless of the weather) in order to be able to complete this requirement.</detail>

winterskills5.3.description: I have been chief cook for at least one meal at winter camp.<detail>Scouts can lead Patrols in preparing at least one balanced and tasty meal while at winter camp.</detail>

winterskills5.2.description:
I have led my Patrol in planning and purchasing meals for a winter camp.<detail>Scouts can lead their Patrols in planning and purchasing food for a winter camp.

Scouts can explain the rationale behind the menu, explaining considerations such as taste, nutrition, budget and food weight and volume.</detail>

seeoneeaward.A1.description: Review your personal progress with your Lair and Scouters.   Think about how you've grown over your time in Cub Scouts.

seeoneeaward.B2.description: Complete **10 stages** () of [[internal:addPage("#adventure-skills");|Outdoor Adventure Skills]] (including stages previously completed as a Beaver). //You may choose to make progress across several Outdoor Adventure Skills or focus on making great progress in a few Outdoor Adventure Skills.//

winterskills3.11.description: I can identify the North Star and three other features in the winter night sky.<detail>Scouts can identify the North Star as well as some of the constellations and/or planets in the winter night sky, and can describe why they can be valuable for navigation and culture.</detail>

aquaticskills1.1.description: I know when to use a PFD (Personal Floatation Device).<detail>Scouts can describe when a PFD is necessary.</detail>

winterskills3.12.description: I have completed a winter hike of at least 3 km.<detail>As part of their Section and/or Patrol, Scouts can complete a 3 km hike in winter conditions.</detail>

aquaticskills1.2.description: I can float for five seconds and glide for five metres on my front and back without assistance.<detail>Scouts can enter a swimming pool and (under the supervision of a lifeguard) demonstrate the water skills.</detail>

aquaticskills1.3.description: I can put my face in the water and blow bubbles.<detail>Scouts can blow bubbles underwater.</detail>

winterskills3.10.description: I have spent a total of two nights at winter camp in a cabin or heated tent (including requirements for previous stages).<detail>Scouts can spend one night at a winter camp in a cabin or heated tent.</detail>

aquaticskills1.4.description: I understand the importance of the buddy system and how it works for swimming and water activities.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate (in practice) the buddy system (selecting a buddy, watching out for their buddy, etc).</detail>

aquaticskills1.5.description:
I know how to stay safe while playing around water.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate awareness of risks by using (and
encouraging others to use) protection such as sunscreen,
UV clothing, hats and sunglasses (where appropriate).</detail>

aquaticskills1.6.description: I can get an object off the bottom in chest-deep water.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate this skill in a pool or a lake.</detail>

winterskills3.13.description:
I have made a winter survival kit that I take with me on all winter activities.<detail>Scouts can make a winter survival kit that is suitable for all winter activities.

Scouts can explain why they have included the items in the kit and how each can be used in a winter emergency, and they can explain why other possible items are not included.

Scouts can describe possible scenarios (lost in the woods, stranded in a vehicle or cabin due to the weather) in which the kit could be used.</detail>

aquaticskills1.7.description: I know three different animals that live in the ocean.<detail>Scouts can name or describe the sea animals.</detail>

winterskills3.14.description: In addition to previous stages, I have made a piece of winter gear or clothing.<detail>Scouts can make a significant item of winter gear or clothing.</detail>

verticalskills5.9.description:
I can set and use passive and natural climbing protection to build both top and bottom climbing pitch anchor point systems.<detail>Scouts can use rocks, trees and man-made objects as anchor points. 

Scouts must inspect natural and man-made attachments for security.

Scouts must use properly mastered and tied knots (bowline, water knot, over hand, full strength tie off, etc.).

Scouts can demonstrate the use of manufactured passive climbing protection: nuts, hexes, stoppers, cams, etc.

Scouts can explain and correctly apply the principles of the anchor building acronym “SARENE-SA” (Solid Anchors, Redundant, Equalized, No Extension, Small Angles).</detail>

verticalskills5.6.description:
I can lower a climber on a top rope down to the ground.<detail>Scouts using a belay breaking device can lower a climber at a controlled rate and in a safe fashion.

Scouts can use proper verbal climbing commands and procedures before, during and at the end of the rappel.</detail>

verticalskills5.5.description:
I have attached a friction (non-moving part) rappel device to a rope and harness and used the device to rappel.<detail>Scouts can properly feed the rope through the rappel device.

Correct attachment by carabiner from the device to the harness is made. 

Proper hand and body position to operate the device is achieved and maintained during the rappel.

Tension by the belay safety rope is not required during the rappel, but a minimum of slack should be in the belay rope.</detail>

verticalskills5.8.description:
I know the safety rules for “bouldering” climbing.<detail>Scouts can explain the rules for bouldering: 
* wear a helmet,
* do not boulder alone or unsupervised,
* do not climb with feet over waist height,
* use a partner to spot climbers, and
* have a crash pad in place.</detail>

verticalskills5.7.description:
I have constructed and climbed in a “Swiss seat” improvised climbing harness made with tubular or tape webbing.<detail>Scouts can correctly size and tie the knots to make a Swiss seat improvised climbing harness.

The harness is to be tied to the body with the correct leg loop and waist tightness.

A complete top rope climb and lower back down is to be made with the harness on.

The Scout climber is to experience full body weight suspended in the harness.</detail>

verticalskills5.2.description:
I can coil a climbing rope using a butterfly and a mountaineer method.<detail>Scouts can tie the coil to a mastery level with consistent coil lengths and a proper whipping or finish.

The coil should be sufficient to be carried in a backpack, slung over one arm and shoulder and over the back and tied off around the body.

The coil must be able to uncoil freely without entanglements or knots and in short order.

The coils must be in order and of constant length and free of any twists.</detail>

verticalskills5.1.description: I can tie these knots: water (tape), double fisherman’s, prussic, clove hitch and bowline.<detail>Scouts can tie the knots to a mastery level with a firm feel to the knot, symmetry with no twists or cross-overs in the knot, with a 5–10 cm tail coming out of the knot.</detail>

verticalskills5.4.description:
I can belay using a friction, (non-moving part) belay device such as a tube or auto-blocking device.<detail>The Scout belayer can provide a continuous belay to a climber from the start to the finish of the climb when the climber unties from the rope.

The knowledge and skill of attaching and detaching the belay device to the rope is not required.</detail>

verticalskills5.3.description:
I can perform a safety inspection of a climbing helmet, harness, rope and carabiners.<detail>Scouts know what to inspect on each of these items for wear, damage, improper working condition and missing components.
* **Helmet**: all rivets and fasteners secure; all webbing in good condition; the shell is without cracks or defects; all buckles present and working; all size adjustment functions working.
* **Harness**: all webbing in good condition with no cuts, defects or abrasion; all buckles present and in good condition with no cracks, defects or burs; all buckle adjustments working.
* **Rope**: rope has no constrictions or blowouts; no mantel fibers showing through the kern; no abraded, cut or melted kern fibers; dynamic properties are intact; rope is the proper length (usually 60–70 metres); rope is not overly soiled by dirt or foreign contaminates such as oils or chemicals.
* **Carabiners**: all working parts present; gate opens freely without sticking; on a locking gate the barrel works freely; no cracks of defects in the material; no metal burs or sharp edges.</detail>

aquaticskills2.1.description:
I can swim with my head in the water.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate this skill under the supervision
of a lifeguard.</detail>

aquaticskills2.2.description: I can swim 10 metres (any stroke) without assistance.<detail>Scouts (under the supervision of a lifeguard) can demonstrate their ability to swim with their head in the water.</detail>

aquaticskills2.3.description:
I know how to put on a PFD by myself.<detail>Scouts can correctly put on a PFD and float test it.
For purposes of comfort, warmer water (such as a swimming pool) is ideal for this demonstration.</detail>

aquaticskills2.4.description: I know how snorkel gear works.<detail>Scouts can explain how snorkeling equipment (snorkel, snorkel vest, wetsuit, fins) works and when a wetsuit may be necessary.</detail>

aquaticskills2.5.description: I have snorkeled in a pool or open water (such as a lake).<detail>Dive shops are able to provide equipment and support this activity with professional instruction if desired.</detail>

sailingskills3.1.description: I can get help if I see somebody in difficulty on the water.<detail>If Scouts see someone in difficulty on the water, they should know to call for help by whistling and yelling.</detail>

sailingskills3.4.description:
I can identify the equipment Transport Canada requires me to have in my sailboat.<detail>Scouts should be able to identify the five essential pieces of safety equipment and have a rudimentary idea of how to use them.
* One life jacket or PFD for each person on board
* One signalling device (whistle)
* One paddle
* One bailer
* One buoyant heaving line of at least 15 m in length
See Transport Canada—Sail boating guide for details on all classes of boats.</detail>

scoutcraftskills5.3.description: I know how to use a camp axe and camp folding or bow saw safely (opening, closing, passing, cleaning, caring for, sharpening, cutting) and have obtained the appropriate permits for these.<detail>Scouts will demonstrate axe and saw skills consistently over a campout.</detail>

sailingskills3.5.description: I can explain what impact I have on the environment while sailing.<detail>Scouts should have an awareness of the fact that sailing can have an impact on the environment and the need to be respectful of the places in which we sail.</detail>

scoutcraftskills5.4.description: I have maintained and used a commercial backpacking portable water treatment device and know the limitations, advantages and disadvantages of the device.<detail>Scouts will demonstrate these skills over a campout or a two-day trail outing.</detail>

sailingskills3.2.description: I can explain why I should not drink the water from the lake, river or ocean I am sailing on.<detail>Scouts need to understand that untreated lake, river or ocean water may not be safe to drink due to bacteria, germs, parasites or chemicals that may be present in the water.</detail>

scoutcraftskills5.1.description: I have built a lean-to shelter and an A-frame sleeping tripod shelter using wood, tied with four lashing knots: square, diagonal, tripod and shear lashings.<detail>Scouts can build both of these shelters, suitable for one person to sleep in.</detail>

scoutcraftskills5.2.description: I have cooked with cast iron cookware (or substitute cookware) by placing cookware in the fire/coals, as well as on top of the fire/coals.<detail>Scouts can cook a meal over a fire or coals using cast iron cookware suitable to feed a minimum of three people.</detail>

sailingskills3.8.description:
I can tie the reef knot, sheet bend, figure-eight and bowline used by Scouts when sailing or when camping.<detail>Scouts should be able to tie four knots within thirty seconds each.
* reef knot
* sheet bend
* figure-eight
* bowline
</detail>

scoutcraftskills5.7.description: I have caught, cleaned and cooked a fish over a campfire (check local regulations for species, size and season prohibitions).<detail>Scouts may use any tools or equipment they can carry in a backpack to accomplish this task. Scouts must follow local regulations with regard to both fishing and campfires.</detail>

sailingskills3.9.description: I can rig my boat and then practise getting into and out of my boat safely.<detail>Scouts will demonstrate that they can rig a sailboat, and get into and out of their sailboat safely on the water from the shore or dock.</detail>

scoutcraftskills5.8.description: I have laid and lit a teepee fire, pyramid fire, star fire and reflector fire.<detail>Scouts are to demonstrate all four of these fires to a level that is suitable enough to warm one person.</detail>

sailingskills3.6.description:
I can identify six types of sailcraft. Scouts should be able to identify or draw the rigging of six types of sailcraft.<detail>
* cat-rigged
* gaff-rigged dinghy
* sloop-rigged dinghy
* sail board
* keelboat
* catamaran
</detail>

scoutcraftskills5.5.description: I have navigated using a magnetic compass bearing (all off trail) 3 km to a predetermined fixed point in a wilderness area.<detail>Scouts are to demonstrate this skill by leading a Patrol on an off-trail outing over 3 km using a magnetic compass bearing.</detail>

sailingskills3.7.description: I can identify the signs of dangerous weather and water conditions.<detail>Scouts need to know and explain how different weather conditions (wind, rain, sun, and cold) can impact a daysail.</detail>

scoutcraftskills5.6.description: I have built a shelter big enough for three,  made of only natural materials found outdoors and rope, and I have slept out in it for at least two nights.<detail>Scouts can construct a shelter suitable enough to keep out wind and precipitation, and the shelter has been used over at least two nights.</detail>

scoutcraftskills5.9.description: I have built an improvised stretcher out of rope, overnight backpacking camping equipment and natural materials found outdoors.<detail>The Scouts are to construct a stretcher suitable to carry the weight of one person.</detail>

campingskills3.10.description:
I can describe how weather can affect our camp.<detail>Scouts can explain the different types of weather likely to occur in the area they plan to travel to, given the time of year.

Scouts can explain what will happen if it rains in the camp area.

Scouts can explain what will happen if it is very hot.

Scouts can explain what extra gear they need to bring (just in case).</detail>

campingskills3.12.description: I can show how to pitch a tent with help of others.<detail>Working with a team, Scouts can demonstrate how to properly pitch a tent.</detail>

campingskills3.11.description:
I can discuss the 7 principles of Leave No Trace applied to a camp.<detail>Scouts discuss a basic knowledge of the principles of Leave No Trace
and how they affect the way groups camp.</detail>

verticalskills1.2.description:
I have been to a jungle gym playground and know how to play safely and cooperatively with others.<detail>Scouts always take turns and share the equipment. 

Scouts do not climb on other people.

Scouts tell adults when they are going to play at the playground.

Scouts do not jump down from high places.</detail>

verticalskills1.1.description:
I know the safety rules for climbing on rocks, trees, fences and man-made structures.<detail>Scouts know to always climb with an adult’s permission and an adult present.  

Scouts do not climb on fences. 

Scouts climb in playgrounds on play equipment - not on inappropriate structures. 

Scouts get permission from an adult before climbing trees.</detail>

emergencyskills2.9.description: I always follow directions from a Scouter.<detail>Scouts demonstrate the ability to follow Scouters’ directions to keep safe, and can explain why it is important to follow directions from an adult.</detail>

emergencyskills2.7.description: I can recognize a warning label on a product and know to leave the product alone.<detail>Scouts can identify the four hazard symbol pictures (explosive, corrosive, flammable, poison) on a number of household products.</detail>

emergencyskills2.8.description: I can check for dangers at an emergency situation.<detail>Scouts can describe how they should look for potential hazards.</detail>

emergencyskills2.1.description:
I have added items to my own personal first aid kit, and I know how and when to use it.<detail>Scouts have added the following items to their first aid kits (made in [badge:emergencyskills1|Stage 1]]) and should be able to describe basic use of the materials in first aid situations:
* 5–10 gauze pads
* 1 roll of medical tape
* triangular bandages
* roller gauzes</detail>

emergencyskills2.2.description: I can keep myself safe in emergency situations.<detail>Scouts can describe what could be done by them in some of the following emergency situations: house fire, earthquake, tornado, flooding, power outage, etc.</detail>

campingskills3.14.description: I can clean up a fire area after camp.<detail>Scouts can clean up the pit, wood pile and area around the fire pit.</detail>

emergencyskills2.5.description: I know where the list of emergency telephone numbers is located in my home and how to call them.<detail>Scouts can verify where the emergency numbers are posted in a convenient location in their homes.</detail>

campingskills3.13.description: I can make a hot drink using a campfire at camp.<detail>Scouts can make a hot drink on an open fire with cooking pots.</detail>

emergencyskills2.6.description: I know how to Stop, Drop and Roll if my clothes are on fire.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to stop, drop and roll.</detail>

emergencyskills2.3.description: I can care for someone who has a minor burn.<detail>Scouts can describe and demonstrate minor burn care: cooling the burn with clean, cool water for at least 10 minutes, or until the burn is cool.</detail>

campingskills3.15.description:
I have spent **seven** nights at camp.<detail>Scouts have spent at least four nights camping while completing this stage.

Scouts have spent at least two consecutive nights at camp while completing this stage.</detail>

emergencyskills2.4.description:
I have made a home escape plan with my family.<detail>Scouts, with help of their families, have made a home escape plan that could include the following:
* fall & crawl in fire and smoke
* two exits from every room
* get out and stay out
* a safe family meeting spot outside the home
* what to do if a stranger is at the door</detail>

paddlingskills5.14.description: I have attained at least the [[https://www.paddlecanada.com/lake-canoe-includes-waterfront-and-canoeing-basics/|Paddle Canada Canoe Basics]] level of paddling certification.<detail>Contact Paddle Canada to determine this requirement.</detail>

paddlingskills5.13.description:
I have completed and logged at least **six** days of backcountry paddling.<detail>Scouts have logged six days of backcountry paddling.

This can include a mix of day trips and overnight trips.</detail>

paddlingskills5.10.description:
I can explain Scouts Canada’s guidelines for paddle sports.<detail>Scouts have reviewed and can explain Scouts have reviewed and can explain Scouts Canada’s Safety
Procedures with particular attention to the Adventure and Swimming
Standards.</detail>

paddlingskills5.12.description: I can help paddlers at [[badge:paddlingskills1|Stage 1]] identify the parts of their paddle and their canoe or kayak.<detail>Scouts working at Stage 5 can teach paddlers at [[badge:paddlingskills1|Stage 1]] to identify the parts of their paddles and their canoes or kayaks.</detail>

paddlingskills5.11.description: I can assist [[badge:paddlingskills3|Stage 3]] paddlers to get back into their swamped watercraft.<detail>Using the watercraft-over-watercraft rescue technique, Scouts can assist [[badge:paddlingskills3|Stage 3]] paddlers to get back into their watercraft.</detail>

trailskills1.10.description: I have attended at least **two** hikes.<detail>As much as possible these can be different types of day hikes, such as in neighborhoods, parks, open natural areas, etc</detail>

campingskills4.5.description:
I can use basic camp tools safely.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to use a tool correctly and are aware of any safety implications. 
*Be able to use a tool correctly to do the job it was designed for 
*Display your skill in using a particular tool</detail>

campingskills4.6.description:
I can store and cook food safely at camp.<detail>Scouts can describe the type of containers best suited for a camp
setting to keep food away from animals.

Scouts can demonstrate the proper methods to store containers
while in camp.

Scouts can demonstrate when and how to use methods such as
hanging food containers to prevent animal access.

Scouts can demonstrate proper food safely in a camp setting.</detail>

campingskills4.7.description:
I can demonstrate how to treat cuts and minor burns and prevent infection at camp.<detail>Scouts can clean and treat wounds using appropriate methods for
the injury.
Scouts can apply an appropriate bandage to a wound to promote
proper healing.</detail>

campingskills4.8.description:
I can explain and demonstrate the 7 principles of Leave No Trace while at camp.<detail>Scouts can name the seven principles of Leave No Trace and apply each of the principles at camp:
*Plan Ahead and Prepare
*Travel and Camp on Durable Surfaces
*Dispose of Waste Properly
*Leave What You Find
*Minimize Campfire Impacts
*Respect Wildlife
*Be Considerate of Others
Further details available at: [[https://www.leavenotrace.ca/principles]]</detail>

campingskills4.9.description:
I can find the best place to pitch a tent at camp and explain my reason.<detail>Scouts can explain what kind of terrain is good for pitching a tent. Examples include: 
*Level ground 
*Rocky ground 
*Near/away/on hill 
*Shady 
*Sunny 
*Close or away from trees</detail>

sailingskills4.12.description: I can demonstrate how to balance my sailboat and can sail the boat flat.<detail>Under direction of the Skipper, Scouts should be able to move body position to balance the sailboat and to keep the sailboat flat.</detail>

sailingskills4.13.description: I have capsized the sailboat and recovered to an upright position.<detail>Scouts will have rocked a sailboat until it capsizes to gain a sense of the critical “heeling point of no return”. Scouts should never jump out of the boat, and they must stay with the boat and help the Skipper recover the boat to an upright position.</detail>

sailingskills4.10.description: Under the direction of the Skipper, I have sailed my sailboat forward for 200 metres.<detail>Under direction of the Skipper, Scouts should be able to sail their boat forward in a reasonably straight line for a short distance. As much as possible, Scouts should do this with another youth. Adults may be a passenger and/or crew.</detail>

sailingskills4.11.description: I can demonstrate how to steer a sailboat going upwind or downwind.<detail>Under direction of the Skipper, Scouts will be able to head up or bear off the wind depending on the wind conditions and direction.</detail>

campingskills4.1.description:
I can demonstrate teamwork while at camp.<detail>Scouts can participate in camp as full members of the Patrol.

Scouts can play a number of roles while on camp and generally add to the wellbeing of the whole Patrol.</detail>

campingskills4.2.description:
I can list the personal gear for standing camp.<detail>Scouts can indicate (in list form) the items of clothing they need to bring with them for various camping activities over a number of days for a standing camp.

Scouts can show consideration of proper clothes provision for wet weather.

Scouts can explain the benefit of the equipment design as it relates to a standing camp. 
*Spare clothing 
*Eating gear 
*Wash gear 
*Wet weather gear 
*Repair equipment 
*Sleeping equipment</detail>

campingskills4.3.description:
I can show how to use group gear safely at camp.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to correctly use any of the individual
items of group gear</detail>

campingskills4.4.description:
I can show proper use, care and maintenance of group gear during and in between camps.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to go about checking and caring for equipment, considering: 
*Safety implications of poor or dysfunctional equipment 
*Keeping personal equipment in working order 
*How to repair items of equipment 
*The quality of different items of equipment</detail>

sailingskills4.18.description: I can toss a throw bag so that someone in the water can reach it.<detail>Scouts should be able to toss throw a throw bag to within 2 metres of a person in the water.</detail>

sailingskills4.19.description: I can swim and demonstrate the HELP and huddle positions while in the water wearing a PFD.<detail>While in the water, Scouts should demonstrate the solo HELP position and the huddle positions with other Scouts for 7 minutes.</detail>

paddlingskills1.12.description:
I have taken part in a short paddling Adventure of at least one hour.<detail>Scouts will have experienced a short paddling adventure.

Scouts only need only be in the watercraft.

If Scouts want to paddle, they may, but Scouters or more-experienced Scouts are in charge of the watercraft.</detail>

sailingskills4.16.description: I can de-rig a sailboat, dry the sails and store all the parts properly.<detail>Scouts, by themselves, should be are able to put all the parts of a boat into proper storage when they are finished with each sailing experience.</detail>

paddlingskills1.11.description: I can get in and out of my watercraft safely.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate that they can get in and out of their watercraft safely.</detail>

sailingskills4.17.description: I have taken part in at least

paddlingskills1.10.description: I know how to contact the emergency services.<detail>Scouts know how to call 9-1-1 or their local emergency number and to request assistance from the nearest adult.</detail>

sailingskills4.14.description: I can get back into the sail boat solo, or with help from the Skipper, if my boat capsizes.<detail>A Scout should be able to right a capsized sailboat with the help of the crew/Skipper, or solo, and demonstrate re-entry over the transom or gunwale.</detail>

sailingskills4.15.description: I can help my Skipper to return the sailboat to the dock or to the beach safely.<detail>A Scout, acting as crew, should be able to assist the Skipper to dock or beach the boat safely, and then lift the boat from the water to dry land storage.</detail>

trailskills4.1.description: I can teach a scout what to pack for a day hike.<detail>Scouts can show other Scouts how to pack the equipment in their pack: heavy items, soft items, last in-first out principle, food items and water.</detail>

sailingskills4.20.description: I have been introduced to self-help procedures and can explain how to perform the HELP position by myself and the huddle position with others.<detail>Scouts should be able to describe when to perform the HELP and huddle positions and what the self-help positions are intended to do in the water.</detail>

trailskills4.7.description: I can keep a map dry and safe from the elements.<detail>Scouts can describe and use the various methods of keeping a map dry and safe: zip-lock bags, laminating, map cases and map coatings.</detail>

trailskills4.6.description: I can teach a scout how to follow a route on an orienteering map.<detail>Scouts demonstrate to others how to follow a pre-defined route on a map.</detail>

trailskills4.9.description:
I can plan and bring appropriate personal gear to use on a hike based on expected weather forecasts for the hiking area.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate methods of obtaining the forecast for the hiking area.

Scouts can show how to prepare for the various weather conditions that may be encountered on the hike.</detail>

trailskills4.8.description: I can locate a waypoint that has been preprogrammed into a GPS unit.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to locate a pre-programmed waypoint.</detail>

trailskills4.3.description: I can show how to care for all my personal hiking equipment needed for a weekend hike.<detail>Scouts can explain the value of maintaining equipment and demonstrate how to check and care for their equipment including: safety considerations, keeping equipment in working condition, checking in advance, simple repairs and cleaning.</detail>

trailskills4.2.description:
I can pack a backpack for a weekend hike.<detail>Scouts can explain the equipment (including group equipment) needed for an overnight hike. Scouts can show how to pack heavy items, soft items, food, fuel, stoves, and their share of team equipment.

Scouts can explain the types of eye protection needed for various conditions, such as: sunglasses, glacier glasses and snow goggles.

Scouts can list and describe the 10 essential items to always have in their pack.</detail>

trailskills4.5.description:
I can use a map and compass together for navigation.<detail>Scouts can plot a hiking route on a map, taking into consideration the terrain and features. Scouts can follow the progress of the hike and mark points as they are achieved.

Scouts can demonstrate the use of a compass to determine bearings for the route.

Scouts can plot locations based on a grid references, calculate distances and changes in height.</detail>

trailskills4.4.description:
I know how to plan for and avoid food allergies in a group hike.<detail>Scouts can describe how to keep food safe for all members of the group and avoid cross-contamination. 

Scouts can explain how to recognize and treat allergies, including anaphylactic reactions.</detail>

winterskills2.10.description: I know to avoid ice or open water without an adult present.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate an understanding of this hazard and know to avoid iced-over rivers, lakes or ponds without adult supervision.</detail>

winterskills2.11.description: I have made a piece of simple winter gear or clothing (wristlet or neck warmer).<detail>Scouts can make a piece of winter gear or clothing and describe its use and value for winter Adventures.</detail>

trailskills4.17b.description: including an overnight<detail>One of the hikes is to be an overnight experience.</detail>

trailskills4.17a.description:
at least **eleven** hikes<detail>Scouts have attended at least eleven hikes  (including those completed at the previous stages) in wilderness-type areas. 

Three of the hikes should be different from those experienced in other stages.</detail>

winterskills4.9.description: I have spent two consecutive nights at winter camp (in addition to requirements for previous stages).<detail>Scouts can spend two consecutive nights at a winter camp. At this stage, it is acceptable for the Scout to spend one of these two nights in a heated cabin or other permanent shelter.</detail>

winterskills4.6.description: I can properly set up my sleeping area to stay warm through the night at winter camp.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate how to properly set up their sleeping areas to stay warm and comfortable while at winter camp.</detail>

winterskills4.5.description: I have put up a tent in winter to sleep in.<detail>As a part of their Patrol, Scouts can put up a tent in winter conditions and sleep in it overnight.</detail>

scoutcraftskills2.1b.description: Round turn and two half-hitch knot

winterskills4.8.description: I have taught a winter skill to a less-experienced Scout.<detail>Scouts can teach a winter skill to a less-experienced Scout.</detail>

winterskills4.7.description: I have used a toboggan or sled to transport equipment.<detail>Scouts can use a toboggan or sled to transport personal and/or Patrol equipment to camp.</detail>

winterskills4.2.description: I have helped purchase food for a winter outing.<detail>With members of their Patrol, Scouts can assist in purchasing appropriate food for a winter outing. They can explain the rationale for the food chosen, addressing considerations such as taste, nutrition, cost and packing weight and volume.</detail>

winterskills4.1.description:
I have participated in a winter sport (different from the sport done in earlier stages).<detail>With members of their Section, family, or through school, Scouts can participate in a winter sporting activity. 

(It is not expected that Scouts will participate in a league or achieve a specific level of proficiency in the given sport.)</detail>

winterskills4.4.description: I have attended a winter campfire.<detail>Scouts can participate in at least one outdoor winter campfire.</detail>

winterskills4.3.description: I have helped cook meals at winter camp.<detail>As part of a team, Scouts can help prepare more than one meal for their Patrol while at winter camp.</detail>

emergencyskills4.10.description:
I can care for my feet while outdoors.<detail>Scouts know how to:
* detect a pre-blister hot spot on a foot
* treat a blister
* identify and prevent trench foot
* select the proper footwear for the activity
* keep toe nails clipped before hiking
* hike in dry socks and footwear</detail>

emergencyskills4.11.description: I can explain how to prevent and treat heat and cold injuries.<detail>Scouts can describe the heat and cold injuries encountered when outdoors and the behaviour, equipment, medical and shelter plans to avoid these.</detail>

emergencyskills4.12.description: I know how to treat and report (if appropriate) insect and animal bites.<detail>Scouts can explain what types of insect and animal bites could happen when outdoors, what the first aid treatment should be and what the follow-up plan should be (if needed).</detail>

scoutcraftskills1.3.description: When outdoors or at camp, I know what is drinkable (safe) and not drinkable (unsafe) water and to check with a Scouter when I am unsure.<detail>Scouts can explain where to get drinkable water at a camp and where not to get water.</detail>

scoutcraftskills1.4.description: I know why it is important to stick to trails when outdoors.<detail>Scouts can explain that they must stay on trails to keep from getting lost.</detail>

scoutcraftskills1.1.description: I can hang a drying/gear line at camp with a half hitch or other knot.<detail>Scouts can hang a line that can hold items for the whole Patrol</detail>

scoutcraftskills1.2.description: I can keep my mess kit clean at camp.<detail>Scouts can properly clean their mess kits with hot water and soap, and properly bleach and rinse.</detail>

scoutcraftskills1.7.description: I can gather dry burnable wood for a fire.<detail>Scouts can find dry wood in the right sizes for a campfire (tinder, kindling, fuel).</detail>

scoutcraftskills1.8.description: I know to tell adults where I am going when outdoors.<detail>Scouts can explain why it is important to always tell an adult where they will be when in the outdoors.</detail>

scoutcraftskills1.5.description: I know three reasons for having a shelter when sleeping outdoors.<detail>Scouts can explain that a shelter is used to keep warm, to stay out of the rain or hot sun, and to stay out of the wind.</detail>

scoutcraftskills1.6.description: I can name three wildflowers by direct observation in a wild field, bush or forest.<detail>Scouts can find and identify three wildflowers growing in the wild.</detail>

scoutcraftskills1.9.description:
I know how to keep a camp clean.<detail>Scouts can keep personal equipment clean and organized.  Scouts can help keep the fire pit, kitchen, sleeping area and dining area clean and free from trash and ensure all patrol equipment is stored in the proper place.

Scouts can explain why a clean and tidy camp is important.</detail>

paddlingskills5.9.description: I have made a personal survival kit as identified in the Field Guide for Canadian Scouting (page 27-28).<detail>Scouts can make a personal survival kit (including signaling devices, first aid items, food items, tinder and a fire starter) that is waterproof and buoyant.</detail>

paddlingskills5.8.description: I can light a fire using no more than three matches.<detail>Scouts can demonstrate the ability to light a fire quickly and efficiently.</detail>

paddlingskills5.7.description: I have participated in a canoe-over-canoe rescue as both the rescuer and the one being rescued.<detail>In a swimming pool or in open water, Scouts can demonstrate the ability to complete a canoe-over-canoe rescue.</detail>

paddlingskills5.6.description:
I can demonstrate how to pack my personal gear so that it will stay dry.<detail>Scouts can properly pack their personal gear so that it will stay dry during a paddling trip.

They have considered options such as Ziploc bags and garbage bags or commercial dry bags and barrels, and can discuss the pros and cons of these options.</detail>

paddlingskills5.5.description: I can demonstrate a self-rescue with my canoe or kayak.<detail>Scouts can swim a capsized watercraft to shore or paddle it (10 m) while sitting in it.</detail>

paddlingskills5.4.description: I can recognize the symptoms of weather-related injuries and know how to treat them.<detail>Scouts know the signs and symptoms and recommended treatment of weather-related injuries such as: hypothermia, hyperthermia, heat exhaustion, sun stroke, frost bite, etc.</detail>

paddlingskills5.3.description: I have participated in creating a menu for an overnight trip.<detail>As a part of their Patrol, Scouts can contribute meal ideas for one each of breakfast, lunch and supper for a menu.</detail>

paddlingskills5.2.description:
I have helped prepare an emergency plan and a float plan with a more-experienced paddler for one of the trips.<detail>With the help of a more experienced Scout or Scouter, Scouts can assist in the completion of a trip emergency plan (as outlined on pages 10–11 in the Field Guide to Canadian Scouting).

Scouts can complete their own float plan that includes their intended route, dates, potential camping locations and intended return date.

Scouts can complete an emergency plan that identifies potential hazards they may encounter, a system for dealing with hazards and a method for contacting emergency services if required.</detail>

paddlingskills5.1.description: I have participated in at least **two** two-day paddling trips.<detail>Scouts have participated in a minimum of two paddling trips that include overnight camping.</detail>
